name: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations
audience: Professionals who use Claude in daily work: analysts, marketers, HR, ops, consultants, PMs. No coding or API experience is needed; the official guide says the credential is not aimed at developers who build against the API or design agentic systems.
format: 60 multiple-choice and multiple-response items in 120 minutes; scaled score 100–1000, pass 720. Each multiple-response item states how many answers to select. Delivered by Pearson VUE, online proctored or at a test centre. Source: official CCAO-F Exam Guide v1.0 (July 2026).

domains.name: Prompting & Task Execution
domains.summary: Writing clear, context-rich prompts for business tasks, breaking big jobs into steps, and iterating instead of starting over. Includes adapting your prompting to the task type: analysis, research, drafting or brainstorming.

domains.name: Output Evaluation & Validation
domains.summary: The heaviest domain: checking outputs for accuracy and completeness, spotting hallucinations, inconsistencies and bias, and deciding when human review is needed. Also covers editing outputs for the intended audience and choosing the output format (artifact, inline or structured data).

domains.name: Product & Model Selection
domains.summary: Choosing the right feature (chat, Projects, Research, artifacts) and the right model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) for the cost, speed and quality you need. Also covers context limits and memory: when to restart, summarize or persist.

domains.name: Workflow Integration & Solution Design
domains.summary: Analysing use cases and fitting Claude into existing workflows, using it for research, planning and process improvement, and keeping humans in the loop where it matters. Includes explaining Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders.

domains.name: Configuration & Knowledge Management
domains.summary: Setting up Projects with instructions and knowledge, managing uploaded files and connectors such as Google Drive and Gmail, and writing good system-level instructions. Includes keeping configurations, knowledge and instructions up to date.

domains.name: Governance, Risk & Responsible Use
domains.summary: Telling appropriate from inappropriate use cases, and handling data sensitivity, regulatory and privacy concerns. Following your organisation's AI policy and understanding the ethical implications of AI use.

domains.name: Troubleshooting & Optimization
domains.summary: Diagnosing underperforming prompts and poor outputs, adjusting based on feedback and results, and making workflows more efficient, for example by using fewer resources on routine work.

scenarios.title: Marketing team drafting campaigns
scenarios.description: You draft launch messaging, adapt copy across channels and keep brand voice consistent through a shared Project. Watch factual claims about the product and any comparisons with competitors.

scenarios.description: You run a Project that answers employee policy questions and helps draft policy updates. The content is sensitive, so current documents, data handling and human sign-off matter most.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an effective prompt
lessons.summary: Claude does its best work when you treat it like a brilliant new colleague who has zero context. Give it the goal, the audience, the background, the constraints, and what 'good' looks like.

sections.heading: The 'new colleague' mental model
sections.body:
Claude can't see your inbox, your company's history, or the meeting you just left, unless you give it that information or connect a tool that can. Anthropic's own test: **show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too.**

Most weak outputs come from weak inputs. A vague request like "write an email about the delay" makes Claude guess the audience, tone, length, cause, and next steps.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.body:
A strong prompt usually includes:

- **Task**: what to produce, stated directly ("Draft a 150-word email...").
- **Context**: background, why it matters, who it's for.
- **Role or perspective** (optional): "You are reviewing this as a skeptical CFO."
- **Inputs**: the documents, data, or notes to work from, clearly separated from your instructions.
- **Constraints**: length, format, tone, things to avoid, deadline-driven priorities.
- **Success criteria**: how you'll judge the result ("A non-technical customer should understand it in one read").
- **Examples** (optional but powerful): a few varied samples of the style or format you want.

sections.heading: Role and success criteria
sections.body:
A **role** focuses Claude's behavior and tone. Even a single sentence such as "You are reviewing this as a skeptical CFO" makes a difference. Put it at the start of the prompt, or in Project instructions if you want it every time.

**Success criteria** come before polishing the prompt. Decide what a good result looks like and how you'll check it ("under 200 words, every number traceable to the attached report, readable by a non-specialist"). Without criteria you can't tell whether a prompt change helped.

sections.heading: Structure with tags and headings
sections.body:
When a prompt mixes instructions with long material, separate them so Claude doesn't confuse the two. XML-style tags work well:

```
Summarize the customer feedback below for our product team.
Group it into themes, count mentions per theme, and quote one example for each.

<feedback>
...paste survey responses here...
</feedback>
```

Tags like `<document>`, `<notes>`, or `<example>` aren't magic keywords. They're clear labels. Markdown headings work too. What matters is that the boundaries are unambiguous.

sections.heading: Examples (few-shot prompting)
sections.body: Showing beats telling. If you want a particular voice or format, paste examples and say what to copy (tone, length, structure) and what **not** to copy (the specific facts). Anthropic's prompting guidance suggests **3–5 examples** for best results, wrapped in tags such as `<example>`, and **varied** enough that Claude learns the pattern instead of cloning one sample. You can even ask Claude whether your examples are diverse enough.

sections.heading: Ask for what you want, positively
sections.body: "Write in plain, flowing paragraphs" works better than "Don't use bullet points." Say why a constraint exists ("this will be read aloud, so avoid lists and symbols"). The reason helps Claude handle cases your rule didn't anticipate.

keyPoints: Context is the biggest lever. Assume Claude knows nothing about your situation.
State the task, audience, constraints, and success criteria explicitly.
Separate instructions from source material with tags or headings.
A few varied examples (guidance suggests 3–5) teach a format or voice faster than adjectives.
Explain the reason behind a constraint so Claude can generalize it.
A one-sentence role and explicit success criteria sharpen almost any business prompt.

gotchas.trap: Making the prompt longer with ALL-CAPS warnings and repeated 'MUST' statements.
gotchas.correct: Add clear context and a reason for each constraint. Calm, specific instructions usually work better than shouting, and heavy emphasis can make Claude over-apply a rule.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Claude remembers details from an unrelated earlier chat.
gotchas.correct: Give the needed context in the current chat, or use a Project or memory deliberately. Never assume it carries over.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a document and writing 'thoughts?'
gotchas.correct: Say what you want: the decision you're making, the angle to review from, and the output format.

lessons.lab: Take a real task from your week (an email, summary, or plan). Write a one-line prompt in claude.ai and save the result. Then rewrite the prompt with task, context, audience, constraints, success criteria, and one example, and compare the two outputs side by side. Note which additions made the biggest difference.

lessons.title: Task decomposition, iteration, and thinking
lessons.summary: Big, fuzzy tasks give generic results. Break the work into stages, review each stage, and refine in the same conversation instead of starting over.

sections.heading: Why decompose?
sections.body:
A prompt like "Write our Q3 strategy deck" bundles research, analysis, structure, and writing into one step. Splitting it gives you a checkpoint after each stage:

- **Step 1:** "Here are our Q3 numbers and goals. List the 5 most important findings, with the data behind each."
- **Step 2:** "Using findings 1, 2, and 4, propose a 7-slide outline."
- **Step 3:** "Draft speaker notes for slides 1–3."

Each step is easier to check, and an error caught early doesn't spread into the final product. This is called **prompt chaining**.

sections.heading: Iterate, don't restart
sections.body:
First drafts are a starting point. Give specific feedback: "Shorter. Lead with the customer benefit. Cut the second paragraph. Keep the call to action." Specific feedback converges faster than "make it better."

When a conversation has gone badly wrong (built on a wrong assumption, or cluttered with dead ends), it can be better to start a fresh chat with a **corrected, consolidated prompt**.

sections.heading: Let Claude think first
sections.body: For analysis, comparisons, and tricky judgment calls, ask Claude to reason before answering: "Before recommending, compare the options against cost, risk, and time to value, then give your recommendation." The Claude apps also let you give the model **more room to think** on hard problems (via thinking and effort settings, which vary by model). More thinking takes more time and usage, so save it for tasks that need it.

sections.heading: Ask Claude to ask you
sections.body: If you're unsure what context matters, say: "Before you start, ask me up to 5 questions you need answered to do this well." It's a quick way to surface missing assumptions.

keyPoints: Chain complex work into stages and review the output of each one.
Give targeted, concrete feedback when iterating.
Start a fresh chat with a consolidated prompt when a thread is polluted.
Ask for reasoning, or give Claude more thinking effort, on analytical or high-stakes tasks.
Let Claude ask clarifying questions when requirements are fuzzy.

gotchas.trap: Asking for the entire 30-page deliverable in one prompt to save time.
gotchas.correct: Decompose it into checkpoints. You'll spend less total time fixing errors.

gotchas.trap: Regenerating repeatedly and hoping for a better answer.
gotchas.correct: Diagnose what's missing (context, example, constraint) and give that feedback directly.

lessons.lab: Pick a multi-part deliverable, such as a project plan. Run it as a three-step chain in one chat: findings, then outline, then draft. After each step, give one piece of specific feedback before moving on.

lessons.title: The AI Fluency 4D framework
lessons.summary: Anthropic's AI Fluency course organizes good human–AI collaboration into four competencies: Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence. The 4Ds aren't a named exam objective, but they are a useful lens for scenario questions, and their vocabulary (such as 'diligence') shows up in official material.

sections.heading: Delegation: deciding what to hand off
sections.body:
Delegation means deciding **whether, what, and how much** of a task to give to AI, based on your goals, the task, and what the AI can and can't do. Good delegation keeps the parts that need your judgment, relationships, or accountability with you.

Example: let Claude draft the first version of a policy FAQ, but you decide which policy positions to take.

sections.heading: Description: communicating clearly
sections.body: Description means telling the AI what you want: the product (what the output is), the process (how to approach it), and the performance (how Claude should behave, such as being a critical reviewer). It's the prompting skill from Lesson 1, seen as a communication skill.

sections.heading: Discernment: evaluating what comes back
sections.body: Discernment means judging the output, the reasoning behind it, and the interaction itself. Is it accurate? Is it complete? Is it appropriate for the audience? Does the reasoning hold up? This links directly to the Output Evaluation domain, the heaviest on the exam.

sections.heading: Diligence: owning the result responsibly
sections.body: Diligence means taking responsibility for what you create and share with AI help: choosing tools thoughtfully, being transparent about AI involvement where it matters, and verifying before you deploy. **You** are accountable for the final work, not the AI.

sections.heading: Description ↔ Discernment loop
sections.body: In practice you cycle: describe, get output, discern problems, describe more precisely, and repeat. Fluency means running that loop quickly and knowing when to stop and verify.

keyPoints: Delegation: what to hand off, and what stays with the human.
Description: communicating product, process, and performance clearly.
Discernment: critically evaluating output, reasoning, and behavior.
Diligence: responsibility, transparency, and verification before use.
Description and Discernment form an iterative loop.

gotchas.trap: Thinking Diligence means 'double-check spelling.'
gotchas.correct: Diligence is about accountability, transparency, and ethical, verified use of AI output.

gotchas.trap: Delegating the final decision on a sensitive matter because Claude's answer sounded confident.
gotchas.correct: Confidence isn't correctness. High-stakes judgment stays with an accountable human.

lessons.lab: Pick one recurring task. Write a short note covering each D: what you'd delegate, how you'd describe it, how you'd evaluate the output, and what diligence steps (verification, disclosure) you'd take before sharing it.

lessons.title: Attachments and prompting by task type
lessons.summary: Uploading a document is only half the job. Place long material before your question, ask Claude to pull quotes before it analyzes, and shape the prompt to the kind of work: analysis, research, drafting, or brainstorming.

sections.heading: Give documents as attachments, not retyped fragments
sections.body:
Claude can read uploaded files directly in a chat or Project, including common formats such as PDF, Word documents, plain text, CSV, and images. Some formats, such as spreadsheets, rely on code execution being available. Uploading the real file keeps the full, original text in view. Retyping or summarizing it yourself first can drop details and add your own errors.

Exact limits on file size, page count, and number of files change over time, so check the current help article rather than memorizing numbers.

sections.heading: Documents first, question last
sections.body:
With long material, put the documents **at the top** and your instructions and question **at the end**. Anthropic's testing found that queries at the end can noticeably improve response quality on long inputs.

When you paste several documents, label each one (for example `<document>` tags with a title or source) so Claude can tell them apart and refer to them.

sections.heading: Quote first, then analyze
sections.body:
For long documents, ask Claude to **first extract the word-for-word passages relevant to your question** (for example into `<quotes>` tags), then answer using only those quotes. This keeps the answer anchored to the text, makes it easy for you to check, and cuts through irrelevant material.

```
<document>...policy PDF text...</document>

First, quote the passages that describe remote-work eligibility in <quotes> tags.
Then, using only those quotes, list who is eligible and any exceptions.
If the document doesn't say, write "not stated".
```

sections.heading: Adapt the prompt to the task type
sections.body:
- **Analysis:** give criteria and ask for reasoning before the conclusion.
- **Research:** state the question, the sources to trust, and ask for sources or quotes behind each claim.
- **Drafting:** give audience, purpose, tone, length, and an example; iterate with specific edits.
- **Brainstorming:** ask for many varied options, defer judgment, then narrow with criteria in a second step.

The same "write me something about X" prompt can't serve all four.

keyPoints: Upload the original file rather than retyping or summarizing it yourself.
Put long documents first and the question last.
Label multiple documents so Claude can tell them apart.
Ask for relevant quotes first, then an answer based on those quotes.
Match the prompt to the task: criteria for analysis, sources for research, examples for drafting, volume then filtering for brainstorming.

gotchas.trap: Asking the question first and pasting a 60-page report below it.
gotchas.correct: Put the report first and the question at the end, and ask for relevant quotes before the answer.

gotchas.trap: Copy-pasting your own summary of a contract instead of attaching it.
gotchas.correct: Attach the original so Claude works from the full, exact wording you can check against.

gotchas.trap: Memorizing exact upload limits as permanent facts.
gotchas.correct: Know the concepts (supported types, large files work, limits exist) and check the help center for current numbers.

lessons.lab: Upload a long internal document you're allowed to share. Ask one question with the question placed first. Then ask the same question with the document first, the question last, and a quote-first instruction. Compare accuracy and how easily you can verify each answer.

lessons.title: Hallucinations and fact-checking
lessons.summary: Claude can produce fluent, confident text that's wrong. Learn the high-risk categories and a verification routine sized to the stakes.

sections.heading: What a hallucination is
sections.body:
A hallucination is output that sounds plausible but isn't supported by facts or by the source you provided. Common forms:

- Invented **citations, quotes, URLs, or statistics**.
- Wrong **dates, names, figures**, or attributions.
- **Overreach**: a summary that states something the document doesn't actually say.
- Fabricated details about **niche or very recent** topics beyond the model's knowledge.

sections.heading: High-risk zones
sections.body:
Be most skeptical about:

- Specific numbers, percentages, and calculations.
- Legal, medical, financial, or regulatory claims.
- Anything recent (after the model's training cutoff) unless web search was used.
- Direct quotes and references, especially when the source wasn't provided.
- Claims about your own organization that Claude couldn't have known.

sections.heading: Reduce hallucinations at the source
sections.body:
- **Ground** Claude in documents: upload them, and ask it to answer only from them.
- Explicitly **permit uncertainty**: "If the document doesn't say, answer 'not stated.'"
- Ask for **supporting quotes**: "For each claim, quote the sentence from the report that supports it."
- Use **web search or Research** for current facts, and check the sources it links.

sections.heading: Verification routine
sections.body:
Scale verification to the stakes:

- **Low stakes** (brainstorm, internal draft): skim for sense.
- **Medium** (internal report): spot-check key claims and every number against the source.
- **High** (external, legal, financial, customer-facing): verify every factual claim against primary sources, have a subject-matter expert review, and keep a record of what you checked.

Open the linked citations yourself. A citation that exists doesn't prove the claim. Confirm the source actually says it.

sections.heading: Stronger checks for important work
sections.body:
Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations adds a few techniques worth knowing:

- **Quotes first for long documents** (Anthropic's docs give >20k tokens as the guide): ask Claude to pull word-for-word quotes relevant to your question, then answer using only those quotes.
- **Cite or retract**: ask Claude to find a supporting quote for each claim and to withdraw any claim it can't support.
- **Best-of-N comparison**: ask the same question more than once (for example in separate chats). If the answers disagree on a fact, treat that fact as suspect and check it.
- **Restrict to the provided sources**: tell Claude to use only the documents you gave it, not general knowledge.

None of these removes hallucinations entirely. Critical information still needs validation against the authoritative source.

keyPoints: Fluent and confident doesn't mean correct.
Highest risk: numbers, quotes, citations, recent events, regulated topics.
Ground Claude in sources and give it permission to say 'I don't know.'
Ask for supporting quotes so claims are traceable.
Match verification depth to the stakes and audience.
Quote extraction, cite-or-retract, and comparing repeated answers all lower risk, but critical facts still need source checks.

gotchas.trap: Asking Claude 'Are you sure?' and treating 'yes' as verification.
gotchas.correct: Self-confirmation isn't verification. Check against primary sources or the provided document.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a citation because it has a real-looking URL.
gotchas.correct: Open it and confirm that it exists and supports the specific claim.

gotchas.trap: Assuming web search means everything stated is sourced.
gotchas.correct: Check which claims are actually linked to sources, and read the sources.

lessons.lab: Upload a 5–10 page report. Ask for a summary with a supporting quote for every claim and 'not stated' where the report is silent. Then verify three claims and every number yourself. Did any summary statement go beyond the text?

lessons.title: Judging quality: rubrics, calculations, bias, and critique
lessons.summary: Beyond 'is it true?', evaluate whether the output is complete, correct in its math, fair, fit for the audience, and logically sound.

sections.heading: Use a rubric
sections.body:
Decide what 'good' means before you read the output. A simple rubric:

- **Accuracy**: are claims correct and supported?
- **Completeness**: does it cover every requirement and input?
- **Relevance**: does it answer the actual question?
- **Audience fit**: tone, reading level, jargon.
- **Format**: length and structure as requested.
- **Risk**: anything that could embarrass, mislead, or expose the organization?

You can give Claude the rubric and ask it to self-review. That's useful as a first pass, but not a replacement for your review.

sections.heading: Checking calculations and data
sections.body:
Language models can make arithmetic or aggregation mistakes, especially when doing math 'in their head' over long tables. Safer approaches:

- Ask Claude to **show the calculation steps** so you can follow them.
- Use **code execution** (where enabled), which runs real code on the uploaded file instead of estimating.
- **Recompute key totals** yourself in a spreadsheet.
- Check that the totals reconcile with the source (row counts, sums).

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.body: Output can reflect biases in training data or in how you framed the question. Watch for stereotyped assumptions, one-sided framing, and uneven treatment of groups. That matters a lot in hiring, performance reviews, lending, and customer treatment. Ask for counterarguments, check that criteria are applied consistently, and never let AI be the sole decision-maker on decisions about people.

sections.heading: Critique techniques
sections.body:
- **Ask for a critique**: "List the three weakest points in this analysis and what evidence would strengthen each."
- **Fresh-eyes review**: paste the draft into a **new chat** and ask for a review as a skeptical stakeholder. A fresh context doesn't carry the original conversation's assumptions.
- **Compare alternatives**: ask for two or three approaches with trade-offs, rather than one answer.
- **Show reasoning**: ask Claude to explain how it reached a conclusion, so you can spot weak steps.

keyPoints: Define a rubric (accuracy, completeness, relevance, audience, format, risk) before reviewing.
Verify numbers using shown steps, real code execution, or your own recalculation.
Check for bias, especially in decisions about people.
A fresh chat reviewing the draft avoids the original thread's anchoring.
Claude's self-review is a helpful first pass, not a final check.

gotchas.trap: Asking the same conversation that wrote the analysis whether it's correct, and accepting its approval.
gotchas.correct: Use an independent review: a fresh chat, a colleague, and a check against the source data.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a total Claude computed mentally across a 2,000-row export.
gotchas.correct: Use code execution or recompute it in a spreadsheet, and reconcile against the source.

lessons.lab: Upload a CSV with at least 100 rows. Ask for a summary table with totals, first with code execution turned off (if you can toggle it) and then with it on. Recompute two totals in a spreadsheet. Then open a new chat and ask it to critique the analysis as a skeptical finance director.

lessons.title: Adapting, comparing, and formatting outputs
lessons.summary: A correct answer can still fail its reader. Learn to adapt output for an audience without changing its meaning, compare alternative drafts fairly, and pick the right output format: inline, artifact, or structured data.

sections.heading: Edit for the intended audience
sections.body:
The same content often needs different versions: engineers want root causes, executives want impact and decision, customers want what changes for them. When you ask Claude to adapt a draft, say who the reader is, what they already know, what they need to do, and what to leave out (internal jargon, speculation, internal names).

Then check the adapted version against the original. Simplifying is where meaning drifts: hedges disappear ("may reduce costs by up to 15%" becomes "cuts costs 15%"), caveats are dropped, and new commitments appear. Facts, figures, and promises must survive the rewrite unchanged.

sections.heading: Compare outputs against criteria, not impressions
sections.body:
Asking for two or three alternatives is a good way to see options, but choose between them with criteria you set in advance: accuracy against the source, coverage of the key messages, audience fit, length, and risk. Longer, more confident, or more polished is not the same as better.

You can ask Claude to compare drafts against your rubric as a first pass. The final choice, and the fact check of the chosen version, stay with you.

sections.heading: Organise and curate before you share
sections.body: Claude can produce more than the reader needs. Curating is part of validation: cut repetition, put the conclusion first, group related points, and remove anything you couldn't verify. If a section can't be traced to a source or a clear reasoning step, it shouldn't go out just because it reads well.

sections.heading: Pick the output format
sections.body:
| Format | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Inline answer** | Short answers, quick explanations, back-and-forth thinking |
| **Artifact / document** | Substantial, self-contained content you'll reuse, edit, or share, such as a checklist, a report, or a small app |
| **Structured data** (table, CSV, JSON) | Output that feeds a spreadsheet or another system, or that must be compared item by item |

Claude typically creates an artifact for content that is substantial and self-contained (usually more than about 15 lines) and likely to be edited or reused, and answers inline otherwise. You can also ask for a specific format. Artifacts need the "Create and edit files" setting (formerly "Cloud code execution and file creation") to be enabled.

For structured data, name the exact fields, say what to enter when a value is missing (for example "not stated"), and spot-check rows against the source. A neat table can hide invented values as easily as prose can.

keyPoints: Tell Claude who the reader is, what they need, and what to omit.
After any rewrite, confirm facts, figures, hedges, and commitments are unchanged.
Compare alternative drafts against criteria you set before reading them.
Inline for quick answers, artifacts for substantial reusable content, structured data for systems and item-by-item comparison.
Structured output still needs spot-checks against the source.

gotchas.trap: Treating a simplified executive version as safe because the original was checked.
gotchas.correct: Re-check it. Simplification often drops hedges or turns estimates into promises.

gotchas.trap: Choosing the longest or most confident of several drafts.
gotchas.correct: Score each draft against criteria set in advance, then verify the one you pick.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a tidy table of extracted values is accurate.
gotchas.correct: Define the fields and a 'not stated' value, then spot-check rows against the source documents.

lessons.lab: Take a technical document you know well. Ask Claude for two versions: one for a frontline team and one for an executive. List every number and hedge in the original, then check that each one survives in both versions. Finally, ask for the key facts as a table with fixed columns and 'not stated' for gaps, and spot-check five cells.

lessons.title: The 4D lens for evaluation: Discernment and Diligence
lessons.summary: Anthropic's AI Fluency framework (Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence) gives you vocabulary for how you evaluate and stand behind AI-assisted work. It's a teaching lens, not a named exam objective, but its ideas run through this domain.

sections.heading: The four Ds in one line each
sections.body:
From Anthropic's AI Fluency course materials:

- **Delegation**: deciding what work humans do, what AI does, and how to split it (problem awareness, platform awareness, task delegation).
- **Description**: communicating effectively with the AI.
- **Discernment**: thoughtfully and critically evaluating AI outputs, processes, behaviours, and interactions.
- **Diligence**: using AI responsibly and ethically, being transparent, and taking accountability for AI-assisted work.

The guide's own sample item calls verifying a cited detail "the diligence step", so the vocabulary is worth knowing even though the exam objectives don't name the framework.

sections.heading: Description: product, process, performance
sections.body:
- **Product description**: what you want: the output, format, audience, and style.
- **Process description**: how Claude should approach it, such as steps to follow or sources to use.
- **Performance description**: how Claude should behave while working with you, for example concise vs. detailed, or challenging vs. supportive.

Good evaluation starts here: you can only judge an output against what you asked for.

sections.heading: Discernment: product, process, performance
sections.body:
- **Product discernment**: is the output accurate, appropriate, coherent, and relevant?
- **Process discernment**: how did Claude get there? Look for logical errors, lapses in attention, or inappropriate reasoning steps. Asking Claude to show its reasoning makes this possible.
- **Performance discernment**: is the way Claude is communicating working for you? If not, change your description.

sections.heading: Diligence: creation, transparency, deployment
sections.body:
- **Creation diligence**: being thoughtful about which AI systems you use and how.
- **Transparency diligence**: being honest about AI's role in your work with everyone who needs to know.
- **Deployment diligence**: taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for the outputs you use or share.

A disclaimer such as "AI-generated, not checked" is not diligence. You remain accountable for what you send.

sections.heading: Interaction modes change how you check
sections.body:
- **Automation**: Claude executes a defined task. Check outputs systematically, often by sampling.
- **Augmentation**: you and Claude think together in back-and-forth. Discernment happens turn by turn.
- **Agency**: you configure Claude to work more independently, setting its knowledge and behaviour rather than exact actions. Checks move to the setup and to review points.

keyPoints: Discernment has product, process, and performance parts: output quality, reasoning quality, and communication fit.
Diligence has creation, transparency, and deployment parts.
Deployment diligence means you verify and vouch for what you share.
Description also has product, process, and performance parts.
Automation, augmentation, and agency call for different review points.

gotchas.trap: Thinking Discernment only means checking the final answer.
gotchas.correct: It also covers the reasoning (process) and whether Claude's way of interacting works for you (performance).

gotchas.trap: Adding an 'AI-generated' label instead of reviewing.
gotchas.correct: Transparency is part of Diligence, but so is verifying and taking responsibility for the output.

lessons.title: Claude's product surfaces
lessons.summary: Know where Claude lives and what each surface is best at: the Claude apps on web, desktop, and mobile for everyday knowledge work; integrations such as Claude for Excel, Claude in Chrome, and Claude Tag in Slack; developer surfaces (Claude Code and the API) that Associates recognise and escalate; and individual vs. organizational plans.

sections.heading: Chat apps: web, desktop, mobile
sections.body:
**claude.ai** (web), the **desktop apps**, and the **mobile apps** offer the core experience: conversations, file uploads, **Projects**, **artifacts**, web search, **Research**, connectors, and more, depending on your plan.

On accounts where it has rolled out (individual paid plans first; Team and Enterprise when admins turn it on), chat and Cowork are merged into **one Claude**: a single conversation where Claude decides whether to answer quickly or to create files, run code, or browse. You don't need to pick a separate mode. For most knowledge work (drafting, analysis, summaries, planning), the chat apps are the default surface.

sections.heading: Integrations: Excel, Chrome, Slack
sections.body:
Integrations bring Claude to where the work already lives. Keep the concepts, and verify current availability before relying on one.

- **Claude for Excel**: an add-in that works inside a workbook. It cites the cells behind its answers and preserves formula relationships when it changes values. Anthropic's guidance is not to use it for final client deliverables without human review or for audit-critical calculations without verification, and to use it only with **trusted spreadsheets**.
- **Claude in Chrome**: a browser extension that can read pages and take actions in the browser on paid plans. **Prompt injection** from web pages is the biggest risk. Claude asks permission before financial sites, admins can allow or block sites, and a separate browser profile is recommended for sensitive accounts.
- **Claude Tag (Slack)**: the Slack integration is now called **Claude Tag**. It is for Team and Enterprise plans (public beta at the time of writing). You `@Claude` in a channel and results post in the thread. Rule of thumb from Anthropic's docs: team work in shared channels is Claude Tag; personal work on your own files is Cowork (now part of the unified Claude app) or Claude Code.

sections.heading: Developer surfaces: Claude Code and the API
sections.body:
**Claude Code** is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: it reads a codebase, edits files, and runs commands. The **Claude API** is how developers build Claude into their own products and automated pipelines.

The Associate credential is **not** for people who build against APIs or design agentic systems. Your job is to **recognise** when a need belongs there (for example, "embed Claude in our customer portal" or "refactor our app's codebase") and **escalate** it to developers or architects, rather than configure it yourself. Drafting a marketing email or a project plan does not need Claude Code.

sections.heading: Plans, conceptually
sections.body:
- **Free**: try Claude with lower limits and fewer features (for example, no Research).
- **Pro, Max, Ultra**: individual paid plans with progressively higher usage and more features, such as Opus and Research.
- **Team / Enterprise**: organizational plans with central billing, admin controls, SSO, and (for Enterprise) advanced security and compliance features such as audit logs and custom data retention. Under commercial terms, customer content is not used to train models by default.

Plan names, prices, limits, and included features change often. **Verify current plans** on Anthropic's pricing page. For the exam, know the **concept**: individual vs. organizational plans, and that organizations get admin governance.

keyPoints: The Claude apps (web, desktop, mobile) are the default surface for knowledge work.
Excel, Chrome, and Slack (Claude Tag) integrations bring Claude to where the work lives. Verify availability and treat outside content as untrusted.
Claude Code and the API are developer surfaces: recognise the need and escalate, don't configure.
Team and Enterprise add admin controls, SSO, and commercial data terms.
Plan details change often. Know the concepts and verify specifics.

gotchas.trap: Recommending Claude Code to a marketing manager who wants help drafting campaign copy.
gotchas.correct: Use the Claude app, ideally a Project with brand guidelines. Claude Code is for software development.

gotchas.trap: Letting an employee use a personal consumer account for confidential company work because it's 'the same Claude.'
gotchas.correct: Use the organization's approved Team or Enterprise workspace, which has admin controls and commercial data terms.

gotchas.trap: Pointing Claude in Chrome or Claude for Excel at untrusted pages or spreadsheets and accepting whatever actions it proposes.
gotchas.correct: Use integrations only with trusted content, watch for prompt injection, and review results before they become deliverables.

gotchas.trap: Trying to wire Claude into a company's product yourself because a stakeholder asked for 'an AI feature'.
gotchas.correct: Recognise this as API or developer work and escalate it to the right technical team.

lessons.lab: List five tasks from your role. For each one, pick the best surface (Claude app, a Project, Claude for Excel, Claude in Chrome, Claude Tag in Slack, or 'escalate to developers') and write one sentence explaining why.

lessons.title: Choosing models and features
lessons.summary: Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus trade capability against speed and cost. Web search, Research, thinking and effort, and artifacts each fit specific jobs.

sections.heading: Model tiers
sections.body:
Claude comes in a family of models:

- **Opus**: the most capable of the three. Best for complex reasoning, nuanced writing, difficult analysis, and long agentic knowledge work. Slower, costs more, and uses more of your limits.
- **Sonnet**: a strong balance of intelligence and speed. A good default for much everyday professional work.
- **Haiku**: the fastest and lowest-cost. Built for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing.

Align the choice with **cost, speed, and quality**: use the smallest model that reliably meets your quality bar, and move up a tier when quality matters more than speed. Anthropic also offers a newer top tier above Opus on some plans; the same trade-off applies. Version numbers change, so learn the trade-off, not the version.

sections.heading: Web search vs. Research vs. thinking
sections.body:
Anthropic's own guidance separates three features:

- **Web search**: straightforward, factual questions that one or two searches can answer, such as recent events, today's prices, or a current policy. Claude cites its sources.
- **Research**: comprehensive information gathering that needs many searches over a few minutes (and, on web and desktop, can use your connected sources). It produces a longer, cited report. It is on paid plans, needs web search on, and uses limits faster.
- **Extended thinking**: complex reasoning that **doesn't** need recent information from the web, such as multi-step analysis, planning, tricky logic, or math-heavy scenarios.

You can combine thinking with Research to pair careful planning with broad gathering. Either way, **check the cited sources**.

sections.heading: Effort and thinking in the apps
sections.body:
In the Claude apps, one model menu controls the **model**, the **effort** level, and **thinking**. Effort runs from Low (routine work) through High (a balanced default) up to Max (the deepest analysis). Higher effort uses more tokens and more of your usage limit.

Some top models **always think**, so there is no thinking toggle for them; if you want a faster, lighter answer, **lower the effort** instead. Turning up effort or thinking on a two-line rewrite only adds latency and cost.

sections.heading: Artifacts and Projects
sections.body:
- **Artifacts** are standalone outputs beside the chat: documents, code, diagrams, simple interactive apps, and visualizations. Claude typically makes one when the content is substantial, self-contained, and likely to be reused or edited. Use artifacts for reusable deliverables, not for a quick conversational answer.
- **Projects** are self-contained workspaces with their own instructions, knowledge, and chat history. Use one when you'll return to the same context repeatedly.

sections.heading: Files and analysis
sections.body: You can upload PDFs, documents, images, and spreadsheets. With **code execution and file creation** turned on (the setting is now labelled "Create and edit files"), Claude can run code to analyze data accurately and create files such as spreadsheets, documents, and slides. Use it for data work instead of relying on mental arithmetic.

keyPoints: Opus = most capable, Sonnet = balanced, Haiku = fastest and lowest-cost.
Use the smallest model that reliably meets the quality bar; align with cost, speed, and quality.
Web search for quick current facts. Research for deep, multi-source investigations. Thinking for complex reasoning that doesn't need the web.
Effort is a dial: higher effort costs more time and usage. On always-thinking models, lower the effort for lighter tasks.
Artifacts for substantial, reusable outputs. Code execution for accurate data work.

gotchas.trap: Using the most powerful model at maximum effort for every quick reformatting task.
gotchas.correct: Match model and effort to the task. A lighter, faster setup is better for simple work.

gotchas.trap: Asking about last week's regulation change without web search and trusting the answer.
gotchas.correct: Enable web search or provide the source, because the model's training data may not include recent changes.

gotchas.trap: Turning on extended thinking to get today's news.
gotchas.correct: Thinking adds reasoning, not new facts. Current information needs web search or Research.

lessons.lab: Run the same complex question (for example, 'compare three pricing strategies for our product given these constraints') with a lighter model at low effort, then with a more capable model at higher effort. Compare quality, time, and usage. Then ask a current-events question with and without web search.

lessons.title: Managing context and memory
lessons.summary: Every conversation has a context limit, and Claude's memory features decide what carries over between chats. Know when to restart, when to summarize, and when to persist context in a Project or memory.

sections.heading: Context window vs. usage limits
sections.body:
Two different limits often get confused:

- The **context window** (length limit) is how much text Claude can consider in one conversation: your messages, its replies, and attached files.
- **Usage limits** cap how much you can use Claude over a period of time, and are shared across Claude surfaces.

Long conversations, large attachments, higher effort, Research, and web search all consume more. With code execution on, Claude can **automatically summarize earlier messages** as a chat nears the limit so you can keep going, though that also uses more of your limit.

sections.heading: Restart, summarize, or persist?
sections.body:
- **Restart** (start a new chat) when the topic changes, when a long thread has drifted or picked up wrong assumptions, or when responses get slower and less focused. Old, irrelevant context can hurt more than help.
- **Summarize** when you need to continue the same work in a fresh chat: ask Claude for a concise summary of decisions, open questions, and key facts, check it, and paste it into the new chat.
- **Persist** context you'll reuse across many chats: put stable reference material and instructions in a **Project**, and let **memory** carry personal preferences and ongoing context. Keep project instructions short and remove files you no longer need.

sections.heading: Memory, chat search, and incognito
sections.body:
- **Memory** stores context from your chats as topics you can view and edit in settings. Each Project has its own memory and, by default, also draws on your account memory; turn off "Use account memory" in a Project to isolate it fully. Pausing memory keeps what's stored; resetting deletes it. On Team and Enterprise, owners control memory for the organization.
- **Chat search** (paid plans) lets Claude look up relevant past conversations when you ask.
- **Incognito chats** are not saved to history or memory. Use them when you don't want a conversation to influence future ones, while remembering that organizational retention rules still apply.

keyPoints: Context window = how much one conversation can hold. Usage limits = how much you can use over time.
Restart when the topic changes or a long thread drifts.
Summarize decisions and open questions to carry work into a fresh chat.
Persist reusable context in a Project; let memory carry personal preferences.
Incognito keeps a chat out of history and memory.

gotchas.trap: Running every task for a month in one giant conversation 'so Claude remembers everything'.
gotchas.correct: Start new chats per task, and keep reusable context in a Project or memory.

gotchas.trap: Re-uploading the same style guide to every new chat.
gotchas.correct: Add it once to a Project's knowledge so every chat in the Project uses it.

gotchas.trap: Assuming incognito exempts a chat from company retention policies.
gotchas.correct: Incognito keeps a chat out of your history and memory; organizational retention and export rules still apply.

lessons.lab: Pick a long chat you've had with Claude. Ask it for a five-bullet summary of decisions and open questions, check the summary for errors, and start a new chat with it. Then decide which parts belong permanently in a Project instead.

lessons.title: Projects, files, and artifacts in real workflows
lessons.summary: Turn one-off chats into repeatable workflows: shared context in Projects, clean file inputs, and artifacts as the deliverable.

sections.heading: Projects as a workspace
sections.body:
A **Project** groups related chats with shared **project knowledge** (uploaded documents) and **project instructions** (custom instructions that apply to every chat in the Project). On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be **shared** with colleagues, which standardizes how a team uses Claude for a workflow.

Examples:
- "Brand Voice" Project: style guide, approved messaging, sample posts, and instructions on tone.
- "Support Macros" Project: policy documents and instructions to cite policy sections and flag cases for escalation.

sections.heading: Designing the workflow
sections.body:
Before building, map the process:

- **Inputs**: where does the information come from (files, connected apps, people)?
- **Claude's steps**: draft, summarize, classify, analyze?
- **Human checkpoints**: who reviews what, and when?
- **Output**: where does it go (document, email, ticket), and in what format?
- **Failure handling**: what happens when Claude is unsure or the case is unusual?

Put Claude where it adds leverage, such as first drafts, summaries, and pattern-finding. Keep humans where judgment, approval, or accountability is required.

sections.heading: Working with files
sections.body:
- Upload the **source of truth**, not a stale copy.
- Prefer text-based files (searchable PDFs, DOCX, CSV) over blurry scans when you can.
- Say which file to use for what: "Use pricing_2026.pdf for prices, and ignore the older deck."
- Very large knowledge sets may be retrieved selectively rather than read in full, so ask Claude to cite which document it used.

sections.heading: Artifacts as deliverables
sections.body: Artifacts let you build and refine a document, table, diagram, or small interactive tool beside the conversation. Teams use them for reusable assets such as a calculator, a checklist, or a formatted report template. Shared or published artifacts should get the same review as any other company content.

keyPoints: Projects = shared knowledge + custom instructions for a repeatable workflow.
Map inputs, Claude's steps, human checkpoints, outputs, and failure paths.
Use Claude for leverage. Keep humans on judgment and approval.
Be explicit about which files are authoritative.
Review artifacts before sharing, like any other company content.

gotchas.trap: Re-pasting the same 10-page style guide into every new chat.
gotchas.correct: Put it in a Project's knowledge and reference it in the project instructions.

gotchas.trap: Automating customer replies end-to-end with no human review, from day one.
gotchas.correct: Start with human-in-the-loop review, measure quality, and only reduce oversight where it's proven safe and allowed by policy.

lessons.lab: Create a Project for one recurring workflow. Add two or three reference documents and write project instructions covering purpose, audience, tone, the format of outputs, and when to flag uncertainty. Run three real tasks in it and refine the instructions after each.

lessons.title: Connectors and integrations (MCP)
lessons.summary: Connectors let Claude reach your tools (drive, email, calendar, chat, CRM) so it can work with live information instead of copy-pasted snippets. They're built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

sections.heading: What connectors do
sections.body:
**Connectors** link Claude to external apps and data sources. Anthropic provides connectors for popular services (for example Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and others), and users or organizations can add **custom connectors** to remote MCP servers (custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic, so use only trusted, approved ones). With a connector enabled, Claude can search, read, and in some cases take actions in those systems, within the permissions of your account.

Two common examples:
- **Gmail**: Claude can search and read mail and can draft, send, reply and forward. By default it asks for your approval before each action.
- **Google Drive**: Claude can search and read Docs, Sheets, Slides and PDFs. It extracts the text, so treat charts and images in those files as content it may not see.

On Team and Enterprise plans, admins can set each connector or tool to always allow, need approval, or be blocked.

sections.heading: MCP in one paragraph
sections.body: The **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Think of it as a universal adapter: a service exposes an MCP server, and Claude (the client) can use its tools. As a business user you don't need to build MCP servers. You do need to know that connectors are how Claude gets **live, permissioned access** to your systems, and that each one expands what Claude can see and do.

sections.heading: Using connectors well
sections.body:
- Enable **only the connectors a task needs**.
- Be specific: "Search my Drive for the Q3 board deck from October and summarize slides about churn."
- Review any **action** (sending an email, creating an event) before confirming it.
- Remember that Claude acts **with your permissions**. If you can see it, a connector may let Claude see it.
- Only use connectors your organization has **approved**. Admins on Team and Enterprise plans can control which connectors are available.

sections.heading: Risks to keep in mind
sections.body: Content from connected sources (emails, web pages, documents) can contain misleading or even malicious instructions. This is called **prompt injection**. Be cautious when Claude reads untrusted content and is also able to take actions. Keep a human confirmation step for consequential actions.

keyPoints: Connectors give Claude live, permissioned access to your tools, built on MCP.
Enable only what a task needs, and use only approved connectors.
Claude acts within your account's permissions.
Confirm consequential actions (send, create, delete) yourself.
Untrusted content can carry prompt-injection attempts.

gotchas.trap: Enabling every available connector 'just in case.'
gotchas.correct: Least privilege: enable the connectors a workflow actually needs.

gotchas.trap: Exporting CRM data to a CSV and uploading it daily when an approved connector exists.
gotchas.correct: Use the approved connector for live, permissioned data. Manual exports go stale and spread copies of the data.

lessons.lab: If your organization allows it, enable one connector (for example Drive or Calendar). Ask Claude to prepare a meeting brief that pulls the meeting details and related documents. Check which sources it used, and review any proposed action before confirming.

lessons.title: Solution design: from use case to stakeholder pitch
lessons.summary: Analyse a use case, pick the right Claude surface for each step, run recurring work as a repeatable workflow, and explain to stakeholders what Claude will and won't do.

sections.heading: Start from requirements, not features
sections.body:
Before choosing a feature, write down the use case:

- **Goal**: what outcome does the team need, and how will you know it worked?
- **Volume and frequency**: one-off, weekly, or hundreds of items a day?
- **Inputs**: which documents, apps, or data, and how sensitive are they?
- **Risk**: what happens if an output is wrong? Who is accountable?

Then decide whether Claude should **augment** the current process (draft, summarize, check) or whether the process should be **redesigned** around what Claude does well. Augmenting is usually the safer first step.

sections.heading: Match each step to a surface
sections.body:
| Need | Good fit |
|---|---|
| Quick question, one-off draft | Chat |
| Same context reused by a team | A shared **Project** with knowledge and instructions |
| A substantial, reusable deliverable (report, table, tool) | An **artifact**, or a Claude Doc or Slides deck you can export |
| Live data from Drive, Gmail, a CRM | An approved **connector** |
| A simple fact that may have changed | **Web search** |
| Broad investigation across many sources, with a cited report | **Research** (paid plans) |
| Analysis inside a workbook | **Claude for Excel**, with cell-level citations |

Research takes longer and uses more of your limit than a quick search, so don't use it for simple lookups. Claude Docs export to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, and Slides export to PowerPoint or PDF, so outputs can land in the tools your team already uses.

sections.heading: Research, planning, and process optimisation
sections.body:
Claude helps at the front of a project, not only at the drafting stage:

- **Research**: gather and compare sources, then verify the key claims before you rely on them.
- **Planning**: turn a goal into a phased plan with owners, risks, and open questions, then have the team challenge it.
- **Process optimisation**: give Claude a description of the current process and ask it to find bottlenecks, duplicated steps, and candidate steps for automation. Treat its suggestions as hypotheses to test with the people who do the work.

sections.heading: Make recurring work repeatable
sections.body: When a task repeats (a weekly status digest, a monthly report), standardize it: one Project or saved setup, a fixed prompt or template, defined inputs, and a named reviewer. Where the unified chat experience is available, **scheduled tasks** can run recurring work for you. A schedule does not replace the human checkpoint. Someone still reviews the output before it is sent or acted on.

sections.heading: Communicate value and limitations
sections.body:
Stakeholders need a balanced picture:

- **Value**: time saved on first drafts, summaries, and analysis; more consistent outputs; faster research. Measure this in a pilot instead of promising it.
- **Limitations**: Claude can be confidently wrong (hallucinations), may reflect bias, has a knowledge cutoff unless it uses search or connectors, and does not own accountability.
- **Controls**: say where humans review, which data Claude can and cannot access, and how errors are caught and escalated.

Overselling ("it's always accurate", "we can drop review") damages trust when the first error appears. Underselling ("it's just autocomplete") stalls adoption.

keyPoints: Define goal, volume, inputs, and risk before choosing a feature.
Chat for one-offs, Projects for shared context, artifacts and Docs for deliverables, connectors for live data, Research for broad cited investigation.
Augment first. Redesign the process once quality is proven.
Scheduled tasks automate the timing, not the review.
Tell stakeholders the value, the limitations, and the controls, and back claims with pilot data.

gotchas.trap: Using Research for a quick factual lookup.
gotchas.correct: Use web search for simple facts. Research is for broad, multi-source investigation with a cited report.

gotchas.trap: Telling leadership Claude is 'always accurate' to win approval.
gotchas.correct: Present measured benefits alongside limitations and the review controls that catch errors.

gotchas.trap: Scheduling a weekly client email that sends without anyone reading it.
gotchas.correct: Schedule the draft, and keep a human review before it goes out.

lessons.lab: Pick one recurring task on your team. Write a one-page design: goal, inputs and their sensitivity, the Claude surface for each step, the human checkpoint, and how errors are escalated. Then write a five-sentence stakeholder summary covering expected value, two limitations, and the controls.

lessons.title: Configuring Claude: instruction layers, Projects, memory, and Skills
lessons.summary: Configuration means Claude starts each task with the right context and behavior, without you re-pasting it. Know which layer to use for which job, and keep the knowledge behind it current.

sections.heading: The configuration toolkit
sections.body:
- **Account-wide instructions** ("Instructions for Claude", under Settings > Your Claude): preferences that apply to all your chats, for example "I'm a finance analyst. Prefer concise answers with tables."
- **Project instructions**: custom instructions scoped to one Project. They apply only inside that Project.
- **Project knowledge**: documents attached to one Project, so every chat in it starts with the same reference material.
- **Memory**: Claude can remember relevant context from past conversations so you don't repeat yourself. It is stored as editable topics that you can view, change, pause, or reset.
- **Skills**: folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads **only when relevant** to a task, such as building a document in your company's template or applying brand guidelines. Skills need code execution to be enabled.
- **Connectors**: give Claude access to live sources such as Google Drive or Gmail (covered in the next lesson).

The old "Use style" menu in Claude chat has been deprecated. To control tone and format, put it in account instructions, project instructions, or a Skill. Feature availability depends on your plan and your organization's settings, so check what's enabled for you.

sections.heading: Choosing the right mechanism
sections.body:
- Applies to **everything you do** -> account-wide instructions.
- Applies to **one workflow or team** -> a Project with instructions and knowledge.
- Needs your **voice or a fixed format** -> describe it (with a short example) in account or project instructions, or package it in a Skill if it's a repeatable procedure.
- A **repeatable procedure** that should be available on demand across contexts -> a Skill.
- Context about **you** that builds up over time -> memory.
- Team-critical **rules** -> explicit project instructions or a shared Skill, never only someone's memory.

sections.heading: Projects in practice
sections.body:
- A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history, knowledge base, and instructions.
- On paid plans, when project knowledge approaches the context limit, Claude switches to retrieval (RAG) so the Project can hold much more material. Retrieval pulls in the most relevant passages, so clear, non-conflicting documents matter even more.
- On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be shared with **Can view** or **Can edit** access. Editors can change instructions and knowledge and manage members, so grant edit rights deliberately.
- Everyone with access to a shared Project can get at its knowledge through Claude. Only add what all members are allowed to see.

sections.heading: Writing good project instructions
sections.body:
Keep instructions short, specific, and explain the *why*:

```
Purpose: Help support agents draft replies to billing tickets.
Audience: Customers; friendly, plain language, no jargon.
Sources: Use only the attached Billing Policy v4. Cite the section.
Rules: Never promise refunds over $100; flag for a supervisor instead,
       because larger refunds need approval.
If unsure or the policy doesn't cover it: say so and recommend escalation.
Format: Greeting, 2-4 short paragraphs, sign-off.
```

sections.heading: Knowledge hygiene
sections.body:
Knowledge management is ongoing:

- Remove **outdated** documents. Old pricing in project knowledge leads to wrong answers.
- Use clear, **versioned file names**.
- Avoid **conflicting** documents, or state in the instructions which source wins.
- Assign an **owner** who reviews instructions and knowledge on a schedule and after policy changes.
- Remove files you no longer need. Smaller, cleaner knowledge is easier for Claude to use well.

keyPoints: Account-wide instructions = all chats. Project instructions and knowledge = one workflow.
Styles are deprecated in Claude chat; express tone and format through instructions or a Skill.
Memory is topic-based and user-controllable; it is not the place for authoritative team rules.
Skills package repeatable procedures that load only when relevant (code execution required).
Curate knowledge: remove stale or conflicting documents, version file names, and assign an owner.
Shared Projects expose their knowledge to every member; Can edit lets members change instructions and knowledge.

gotchas.trap: Looking for the "Use style" menu to set tone in Claude chat.
gotchas.correct: That menu is deprecated. Describe tone and format in account or project instructions, or use a Skill.

gotchas.trap: Leaving last year's price list in project knowledge alongside the new one.
gotchas.correct: Remove or clearly mark outdated documents so Claude doesn't mix them up.

gotchas.trap: Relying on memory to carry critical, authoritative business rules for a team.
gotchas.correct: Put team rules in a shared Project's instructions (or a Skill) where they're explicit, reviewable, and consistent.

gotchas.trap: Giving every member of a shared Project "Can edit" access by default.
gotchas.correct: Most users only need Can view. Edit rights let people change instructions and knowledge for everyone.

Then create a Project for one workflow using the instruction template above, attach one current policy document, and test it with a request the policy doesn't cover. Check that Claude flags the gap instead of guessing.

lessons.title: Connectors, memory controls, and keeping configurations current
lessons.summary: Connectors give Claude live access to your tools; memory carries context between chats. Both are configuration you have to manage, alongside a routine for keeping instructions and knowledge current.

sections.heading: Connectors as knowledge sources
sections.body:
- Connectors such as **Google Drive** and **Gmail** let Claude search and read your live content instead of you uploading copies.
- Access **mirrors your existing permissions**: Claude can only reach what you can already reach.
- The Drive connector reads Docs, Sheets, Slides and PDFs as text. The Gmail connector can search, read, draft, send, reply and forward, and by default asks for your approval before each action.
- On Team and Enterprise plans, admins can set each connector or tool to **Always allow**, **Needs approval**, or **Blocked**.
- Custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic. Only add ones from sources you trust.

**Upload vs. connect:** upload a fixed, approved reference (a signed policy version) to project knowledge. Connect when Claude needs the current state of a source that changes often. Turn off connectors a task doesn't need; they add noise and use more of your limits.

sections.heading: How memory works
sections.body:
- Memory is stored as individual **topics** that you can view and edit (Settings > Your Claude).
- **Each Project has its own memory** and also uses your account memory. Turn off "Use account memory" in a Project to isolate it completely, for example for a confidential client engagement.
- **Pausing** memory keeps what's already saved; **resetting** deletes it all.
- Sensitive topics are excluded unless you opt in, and some categories (such as government IDs and financial account numbers) are never saved.
- **Incognito chats** are not saved to history or memory and are excluded from chat search. They are only available outside Projects, and on Team and Enterprise they still follow the organization's retention and export settings.
- On Team and Enterprise, Owners control memory for the whole organization, and they cannot view members' memories.

sections.heading: Maintaining configurations
sections.body:
Configurations drift. A Project that was right in January can be wrong by June.

- **Trigger reviews** on events (new policy, price change, reorg), not just on a calendar.
- **Replace, don't append**: when a document is superseded, remove the old version or clearly mark which one wins in the instructions.
- **Re-test** after changes: keep a few test prompts with known good answers and run them after you edit instructions or knowledge.
- **Keep instructions short**: long, accumulated instructions contradict themselves and use up context.
- **Name an owner** and record what changed and why.

keyPoints: Connectors give live access and mirror the user's own permissions.
Upload stable approved references; connect sources that change often.
Each Project has its own memory; turn off "Use account memory" to fully isolate it.
Pause keeps memories; reset deletes them. Incognito works only outside Projects.
Review configurations when the underlying facts change, and re-test with known prompts.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a connector gives Claude access to everything in the company Drive.
gotchas.correct: Connector access mirrors the signed-in user's permissions.

gotchas.trap: Pausing memory to delete what Claude has learned about you.
gotchas.correct: Pausing keeps existing memories. Reset (or edit topics) to remove them.

gotchas.trap: Opening an incognito chat inside a client Project to keep it out of memory.
gotchas.correct: Incognito is only available outside Projects. Inside a Project, isolate project memory by turning off "Use account memory".

gotchas.trap: Appending a new policy file without removing the old one.
gotchas.correct: Replace the superseded file, or state explicitly which version wins.

lessons.lab: Pick one Project you use. List every knowledge file with its date and owner, remove anything superseded, and add a line to the instructions naming the authoritative source. Write three test prompts with known correct answers and run them before and after the cleanup.

lessons.title: Data sensitivity and responsible use
lessons.summary: Know what you're allowed to share with Claude, in which workspace, and under which policy. Responsible use protects customers, colleagues, and your organization.

sections.heading: Classify before you paste
sections.body:
Before uploading or pasting, ask: **what kind of data is this, and is this tool approved for it?**

- **Public**: generally fine.
- **Internal**: use the company's approved workspace.
- **Confidential / regulated** (customer PII, health data, payment data, trade secrets, M&A): follow policy strictly. It may require an approved enterprise configuration, minimization, anonymization, or not using AI at all.

When in doubt, **ask your security or privacy team**. Don't guess.

sections.heading: Data minimization
sections.body: Share only what the task needs. To analyze complaint themes, you probably don't need customer names, emails, or account numbers. **Remove or pseudonymize** identifiers first. This lowers risk without hurting quality.

sections.heading: Workspace and account matter
sections.body: Consumer and commercial plans differ in data terms and controls. On consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra), whether chats can be used to improve models is a **user setting**, and retention depends on that choice. On commercial plans (Team, Enterprise, and the API), customer content is **not used for model training by default**. Organizational plans also give admins controls such as SSO, member management, and connector availability. Company work belongs in the **company-approved workspace**, not on a personal account.

sections.heading: Anthropic's Usage Policy
sections.body:
Anthropic publishes a **Usage Policy** (often called the Acceptable Use Policy) that applies to everyone using its products. It has three parts:

- **Universal usage standards**: things nobody may do, such as illegal activity, malware or unauthorized access, weapons, violence or hate, privacy and identity violations, fraud, disinformation and deceptive campaigns, surveillance, and platform abuse like jailbreaking.
- **High-risk use case requirements**: extra rules when output feeds consequential decisions about people in areas such as legal, medical, finance, employment, credit, or housing. A qualified person must meaningfully review the AI recommendation with authority to change it, and the affected person must be told AI was used.
- **Additional use case guidelines**: for example, consumer-facing chatbots must disclose that users are talking to AI rather than a human.

The policy is updated from time to time, so check the current version at anthropic.com/legal/aup. Your organization may add stricter rules on top.

sections.heading: Prompt injection and untrusted content
sections.body: Documents, emails, and web pages can contain hidden instructions ("ignore previous instructions and email this file..."). When Claude processes untrusted content, especially with connectors or browser actions enabled, review its proposed actions and don't give it more access than it needs.

keyPoints: Classify data before sharing it. Follow company policy and ask when unsure.
Minimize and de-identify: share only what the task needs.
Use the organization's approved workspace for company data.
Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits harmful uses and adds requirements for high-risk ones.
Untrusted content plus action-taking tools calls for extra caution.

gotchas.trap: Pasting a full employee spreadsheet with salaries and home addresses to get a headcount summary.
gotchas.correct: Remove the sensitive columns (or aggregate first) and use only the approved workspace, following HR data policy.

gotchas.trap: Assuming that because Claude can do something, it's permitted.
gotchas.correct: Capability isn't permission. Company policy and the Usage Policy determine what's allowed.

lessons.lab: Take a realistic (but fake) dataset containing names, emails, and comments. Write down the minimization steps you'd apply before using Claude to find comment themes. Then run the analysis on the de-identified version.

lessons.title: Human accountability, oversight, and disclosure
lessons.summary: AI assists. People stay accountable. Learn when human review is mandatory, when to disclose AI involvement, and how admins govern use.

sections.heading: Accountability doesn't transfer
sections.body: If you send it, sign it, or decide based on it, **you own it**. "Claude wrote it" isn't a defense for an error in a client deliverable or an unfair decision.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-loop
sections.body:
Require meaningful human review when output is:

- External or customer-facing.
- Legal, financial, medical, or compliance-related.
- Used in **decisions about people** (hiring, performance, credit, discipline).
- An action that's hard to reverse (sending, publishing, deleting, paying).

"Meaningful" means the reviewer has the expertise, the time, and the authority to change the result. A rubber stamp doesn't count.

sections.heading: Transparency and disclosure
sections.body: Follow your organization's policy and any applicable rules about disclosing AI involvement. Disclosure is usually expected when the audience would reasonably want to know, such as published content, customer interactions with an AI agent, or academic and professional work with disclosure norms. Never present AI-generated content as a human's personal testimony, or as verified when it wasn't.

sections.heading: Admin and organizational controls
sections.body: On organizational plans, admins (Owners) set guardrails for everyone: members and roles, SSO, which connectors and tools are allowed, need approval, or are blocked, and org-wide settings for features such as memory and skills. Some controls, such as SCIM provisioning, audit logs, a Compliance API, and custom data retention, are Enterprise features. As an associate-level user, know that these controls exist and who sets them, follow them, and escalate requests (for example, a new connector) through the proper channel instead of working around them.

keyPoints: The human who uses the output is accountable for it.
Require meaningful human review for external, regulated, people-affecting, or irreversible outputs.
Disclose AI involvement according to policy and audience expectations.
Admins govern features, connectors, members, and data settings. Don't work around them.
AI shouldn't be the sole decision-maker on decisions that significantly affect people.

gotchas.trap: Using Claude to rank job candidates and sending rejections automatically.
gotchas.correct: Use Claude to help organize information at most. Humans make the decisions, using consistent, fair criteria and following legal and HR policy.

gotchas.trap: Installing an unapproved third-party connector because IT approval is slow.
gotchas.correct: Request it through the proper channel. Shadow integrations create security and compliance risk.

lessons.lab: For one of your workflows, write a one-paragraph 'AI use note' covering what Claude does, who reviews it, what gets disclosed and to whom, and which data is never shared.
