lessons.title: Usage Policy, data terms, and who controls what
lessons.summary: A practical map of three governance layers: Anthropic's Usage Policy, the data terms of the plan you're on, and the admin controls your organization sets. Know what each layer decides and what you do as a user.

sections.heading: Layer 1: the Usage Policy
sections.body:
The Usage Policy applies to every user and every plan. Its **universal standards** prohibit uses such as creating malware, fraud, surveillance, privacy and identity violations, disinformation, and trying to jailbreak or abuse the platform.

Its **high-risk requirements** apply when Claude's output informs decisions that significantly affect people, such as hiring, lending, housing, insurance, or legal and medical matters:

- **Human-in-the-loop**: a qualified person meaningfully reviews the AI recommendation and has the authority to change it.
- **Disclosure**: the affected person is clearly told AI was used. Naming the specific tool isn't required.

Separately, a **consumer-facing chatbot** must tell users they're interacting with AI, not a human.

sections.heading: Layer 2: plan data terms
sections.body:
- **Consumer plans** (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra): each user chooses whether chats may be used for model training, and retention depends on that choice.
- **Commercial plans** (Team, Enterprise, API): customer content isn't used to train models by default under commercial terms.

Even on a commercial plan, your **company's data policy** still decides what may be shared. Commercial terms reduce risk; they don't make restricted data fair game.

sections.heading: Layer 3: organization admin controls
sections.body:
Owners and admins on Team and Enterprise plans configure the workspace for everyone:

- **Identity**: SSO (Team and Enterprise); SCIM user provisioning on Enterprise.
- **Connectors and tools**: each can be set to always allow, need approval, or blocked. Enterprise custom roles can restrict them further.
- **Features**: org-level settings for things like memory, skills, browser use, and available models.
- **Oversight**: audit logs, a Compliance API, and custom data retention on Enterprise.

Admins can turn memory off org-wide, but they can't read members' individual memories.

sections.heading: What the user does
sections.body:
You don't configure these layers, but you work inside them:

1. Classify the data and confirm the workspace is approved for it.
2. Remove or anonymize identifiers the task doesn't need. Telling Claude "don't keep this" isn't a control.
3. Never paste secrets: passwords, API keys, tokens, or credentials.
4. Keep a qualified human in charge of consequential decisions and disclose AI use where required.
5. If a control blocks you, ask the admin or follow the approval process. Don't route around it.

keyPoints: Three layers govern use: Anthropic's Usage Policy, your plan's data terms, and your organization's admin controls and policy.
High-risk uses need meaningful review by a qualified human with authority to change the result, plus disclosure to the affected person.
Consumer-facing chatbots must disclose that users are talking to AI.
Commercial plans don't train on customer content by default, but company data policy still applies.
Admins control connectors, features, and identity settings. Users follow and escalate; they don't work around controls.

gotchas.trap: "We're on Enterprise, so our data isn't used for training, so I can upload anything."
gotchas.correct: Training terms are one factor. Company classification rules, minimization, and approvals still decide what may be shared.

gotchas.trap: Pasting an API key into a chat so Claude can debug a script.
gotchas.correct: Never share secrets. Redact them with a placeholder and rotate any secret that was exposed.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the admin can read your memory or chats, so you don't need to worry about what you store.
gotchas.correct: Governance doesn't replace your own judgment. Don't put secrets or unapproved personal data into chats, memory, or project knowledge at all.

lessons.lab: Draw a three-row table for your team: Usage Policy, plan data terms, and org admin controls. For each row, list one rule that affects your daily work and who you'd ask about it. Then check the current Usage Policy at anthropic.com/legal/aup and note whether any of your workflows fall into a high-risk area.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting playbook
lessons.summary: When output disappoints, diagnose the cause before changing anything. Most problems trace back to missing context, an unclear spec, overloaded conversations, or the wrong model or feature.

sections.heading: Symptom → likely cause → fix
sections.body:
- **Generic or vague output** → missing context or success criteria → add audience, purpose, and an example.
- **Too long or wordy** → no length or format spec → set a length ("under 120 words") and format. If you always want brevity, put that preference in account or project instructions.
- **Ignores an instruction** → instruction buried, conflicting, or unexplained → move it up front, remove conflicts, explain why it matters.
- **Wrong format** → no example → show the exact format.
- **Made-up facts** → not grounded → provide sources, permit "not stated," and use web search.
- **Forgets earlier details in a long chat** → long or cluttered context → summarize and start a fresh chat, or move stable context into a Project.
- **Slow responses / hitting limits** → heavy model, high effort or extra features on simple tasks, huge files, very long threads → use a lighter model or lower effort, trim inputs, start new chats.

sections.heading: Long conversations
sections.body:
Every message in a chat adds to the context Claude processes. Very long threads can dilute focus and use up usage limits faster. Good habits:

- **One task per chat** where practical.
- When a chat gets long or starts drifting, ask Claude for a **summary of decisions, constraints and open items**, check it, then start a new chat with that summary.
- Put persistent reference material in **Project knowledge**, rather than re-uploading it into one ever-growing thread.
- With code execution on, Claude can **automatically summarise earlier messages** as a chat nears the context limit. That keeps the chat going, but it is not a substitute for a clean restart when the thread has drifted, and it uses more of your limit.

sections.heading: Usage limits
sections.body: Usage limits and length limits are different things. **Usage limits** cap how much you can use Claude over time (a session window that starts with your first message, plus weekly limits, shared across Claude apps). The **length limit** is the context window of a single conversation. Ways to stretch usage: choose a lighter model or lower effort for simple tasks, avoid re-sending large files, keep chats focused, and batch related questions into one well-structured message. Exact limits vary by plan and change over time, so check the current help-center details for your plan.

sections.heading: Change one thing at a time
sections.body: When you're refining a prompt or Project instructions, change **one variable**, test on the same few representative examples, and keep what works. Random rewrites make it hard to know what fixed (or broke) the result.

keyPoints: Diagnose first: context, spec, conflicting instructions, grounding, or context length.
Fix verbosity with an explicit length and format, and put a lasting brevity preference in account or project instructions.
Summarize and restart long, cluttered chats. Keep stable context in Projects.
Save usage by matching model and features to the task and trimming inputs.
Change one variable at a time and test on representative examples.

gotchas.trap: Responding to an ignored instruction by repeating it in capitals three times.
gotchas.correct: Check for conflicting instructions, put the rule where it's clear, and explain the reason.

gotchas.trap: Switching to the most powerful model to fix output that lacks company context.
gotchas.correct: A bigger model can't know facts you didn't give it. Add the context first.

gotchas.trap: Picking the deprecated "Concise" style in claude.ai to shorten answers.
gotchas.correct: Styles are no longer offered in Claude chat. State the length and format in the prompt, or put the preference in account or project instructions.

lessons.lab: Recreate three bad outputs on purpose (vague, too long, ignoring a rule). For each, write the diagnosis and apply exactly one fix. Record which fix resolved it.

lessons.title: Usage limits and large tasks
lessons.summary: Know the difference between usage limits and the context window, what eats into each, and how to split a big job into steps so it fits and stays accurate.

sections.heading: Two different limits
sections.body:
- **Usage limits** cap how much you use Claude over time: a session window that starts with your first message, plus weekly limits. They are shared across Claude on the web, desktop and Claude Code.
- **Length limit** is the **context window**: how much one conversation can hold (messages, files, tool results).

Hitting a usage limit means *wait or reduce consumption*. Hitting the length limit means *start a new chat or reduce what's in this one*. Exact numbers vary by plan and change, so check the current help article rather than memorising them.

sections.heading: What uses more of your limit
sections.body:
- Long messages and large attachments
- Long conversations (the whole history is processed each turn)
- Research and web search
- Higher effort settings and thinking
- Artifacts and multi-step tasks
- Connectors and tools you have switched on but don't need

**Project knowledge is cached**, so reusing it costs less than re-uploading the same file into new chats. The cache expires after a period of inactivity.

sections.heading: Optimise without losing quality
sections.body:
- Match the model and effort to the task: a lighter model or lower effort for routine drafting, the most capable settings for hard analysis.
- Turn off web search and connectors you don't need for this task.
- Batch related questions into one well-structured message and give the context up front.
- Keep project instructions short and remove knowledge files you no longer use.
- Start a fresh chat (with a summary) instead of dragging a long thread forward.

sections.heading: Split large tasks
sections.body:
A 60-page report or a 40-file review in one prompt is slow, expensive and hard to check. Break it into steps:

1. **Plan**: ask Claude for an outline or a list of sub-tasks.
2. **Execute in chunks**: one section, chapter or batch per message (or per chat), using the same instructions.
3. **Check each output** before moving on, so errors don't compound.
4. **Assemble**: combine the checked pieces and ask for a final consistency pass.

Keep shared instructions and reference files in a Project so every chunk gets the same context without re-uploading.

keyPoints: Usage limits (session window plus weekly) are not the same as the context window of one chat.
Long chats, big files, Research, web search, higher effort and artifacts all use more of your limit.
Project knowledge is cached, so reuse it instead of re-uploading files.
Right-size model and effort, turn off unneeded tools, and batch related questions.
Split big jobs into plan, chunk, check and assemble steps, with shared context in a Project.

gotchas.trap: Treating a usage-limit message as a sign the chat is too long, and only starting a new chat.
gotchas.correct: A usage limit is about consumption over time. Reduce what each request uses (model, effort, tools, attachments) or wait for the window to reset.

gotchas.trap: Uploading a huge document set into one chat and asking for the whole deliverable in one go.
gotchas.correct: Plan first, then work in chunks you can check, with the shared material in Project knowledge.

gotchas.trap: Relying on automatic context management to rescue a chat that has drifted off course.
gotchas.correct: Auto-summarising keeps a long chat going, but it still uses more of your limit. Restart with a checked summary when the thread has drifted.

lessons.lab: Take a large task you'd normally do in one prompt (for example, summarising ten meeting transcripts). Ask Claude for a step plan, run it in three or more chunks inside a Project, check each chunk, then assemble. Note where checking caught an issue, and compare how quickly you reached your limit with a one-shot attempt.

flashcards.front: What's the single biggest lever for improving Claude's output?
flashcards.back: Context: who it's for, why, background, constraints, and what good looks like. Treat Claude like a brilliant new colleague with zero context.

flashcards.front: Name the core components of a strong prompt.
flashcards.back: Task, context, (optional) role, inputs, constraints, success criteria, and (optional) examples.

flashcards.front: Why use XML-style tags like <document> in a prompt?
flashcards.back: To separate instructions from source material clearly, so Claude doesn't confuse the two. The tag names are labels, not magic keywords.

flashcards.front: What is few-shot prompting?
flashcards.back: Including examples of the desired output so Claude copies the pattern (tone, format). Guidance suggests 3–5 varied examples, wrapped in tags like <example>, and saying what to copy and what not to.

flashcards.front: Why explain the reason behind a constraint?
flashcards.back: The reason lets Claude generalize the rule to cases you didn't anticipate (e.g., 'this will be read aloud, so avoid symbols').

flashcards.front: What is prompt chaining?
flashcards.back: Splitting a complex task into sequential steps, each with its own prompt and a review checkpoint, so errors are caught early.

flashcards.front: When should you start a new chat rather than keep iterating?
flashcards.back: When the thread is built on a wrong assumption or cluttered with dead ends. Start fresh with a corrected, consolidated prompt.

flashcards.front: A quick way to surface missing context before Claude starts?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to ask you clarifying questions first (e.g., 'ask me up to 5 questions before starting').

flashcards.front: What are the 4Ds of AI Fluency?
flashcards.back: Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Delegation means…
flashcards.back: Deciding whether, what, and how much work to hand to AI, based on goals, task, and AI capabilities. Judgment and accountability stay with you.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Description means…
flashcards.back: Communicating clearly what you want: the product, the process, and the performance (how the AI should behave).

flashcards.front: Why is 'write in flowing paragraphs' better than 'don't use bullets'?
flashcards.back: Positive instructions say what to do and steer behavior more reliably than prohibitions.

flashcards.front: Where should your question go when you give Claude a long document?
flashcards.back: At the end, after the document. Documents first, query last tends to improve answer quality on long inputs.

flashcards.front: What is the quote-first technique for long documents?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to extract the word-for-word passages relevant to your question (e.g., in <quotes> tags) before answering, then base the answer on those quotes.

flashcards.front: Why attach the original file instead of pasting your own summary of it?
flashcards.back: Claude then works from the full, exact text. Your summary can drop details or introduce errors, and the answer can't be checked against the source.

flashcards.front: How much does a role statement need to be?
flashcards.back: Even a single sentence (e.g., 'You are a skeptical CFO reviewing this plan') focuses Claude's behavior and tone.

flashcards.front: What should you have before refining a prompt?
flashcards.back: Success criteria (what good looks like), a way to test against them, and a first draft to improve.

flashcards.front: How should a brainstorming prompt differ from an analysis prompt?
flashcards.back: Brainstorming: ask for many varied ideas and defer judgment, then filter. Analysis: give explicit criteria and ask for reasoning before the conclusion.

flashcards.front: When chaining a task, what do you do between steps?
flashcards.back: Review the intermediate output and correct it before feeding it to the next step, so an early error doesn't spread.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Discernment means…
flashcards.back: Critically evaluating the AI's output, its reasoning, and its behavior for accuracy, quality, and appropriateness.

flashcards.front: What is a hallucination?
flashcards.back: Plausible-sounding output that isn't supported by facts or the provided source, e.g., invented citations, wrong figures, or overreaching summaries.

flashcards.front: Name four high-risk categories for hallucinations.
flashcards.back: Specific numbers or statistics, quotes and citations, recent events beyond the training cutoff, and legal, medical, financial, or regulatory claims.

flashcards.front: Prompt technique to make summaries traceable?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to provide a supporting quote from the source for each claim, and to say 'not stated' when the source is silent.

flashcards.front: Is asking 'Are you sure?' a valid verification step?
flashcards.back: No. Self-confirmation isn't verification. Check claims against primary sources or the provided document.

flashcards.front: A citation has a real-looking URL. Is the claim verified?
flashcards.back: No. Open it and confirm the source exists and actually supports that specific claim.

flashcards.front: How should verification depth relate to the stakes?
flashcards.back: Proportionally: skim for brainstorms, spot-check internal reports, and fully verify plus get expert review for external, legal, or financial content.

flashcards.front: Most reliable way to get accurate totals from a large spreadsheet?
flashcards.back: Use code execution / analysis (real computation) and reconcile key totals yourself. Don't rely on the model's mental arithmetic.

flashcards.front: Why review a draft in a fresh chat?
flashcards.back: A new context isn't anchored on the original conversation's assumptions, so it gives a more independent critique.

flashcards.front: Six rubric dimensions for evaluating output?
flashcards.back: Accuracy, completeness, relevance, audience fit, format, and risk.

flashcards.front: Is Claude's self-review enough for high-stakes content?
flashcards.back: No. It's a useful first pass, but high-stakes content needs independent human or expert review against sources.

flashcards.front: Where is bias review most critical?
flashcards.back: In decisions about people (hiring, performance, lending, customer treatment) and in one-sided framing of contested topics.

flashcards.front: Technique to expose weaknesses in an analysis?
flashcards.back: Ask for the weakest points and the evidence that would strengthen them, or for counterarguments and alternative approaches with trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Why ask Claude to show its reasoning?
flashcards.back: So you can inspect the steps, spot faulty logic or assumptions, and check calculations.

flashcards.front: Web search was on. Are all claims in the answer sourced?
flashcards.back: Not necessarily. Check which claims are tied to citations and read those sources.

flashcards.front: Summary 'overreach' means…
flashcards.back: The summary states conclusions or details the source doesn't actually contain.

flashcards.front: How do you give Claude 'permission to be uncertain'?
flashcards.back: Say so explicitly: 'If you're not sure, or the document doesn't say, say so instead of guessing.'

flashcards.front: What does it mean if Claude gives different answers to the same factual question across runs?
flashcards.back: Inconsistency is a hallucination signal (the best-of-N check). Treat that fact as suspect and verify it against an authoritative source.

flashcards.front: Technique for questions about a very long document?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes relevant to the question first, then answer using only those quotes.

flashcards.front: What is the 'cite or retract' technique?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude to find a supporting quote for each claim and to withdraw any claim it can't support from the source.

flashcards.front: Is Claude's self-reported confidence a reliable accuracy signal?
flashcards.back: No. Confidence ratings and confident tone don't show a claim is correct. Check specific details against the authoritative source.

flashcards.front: When does Claude typically create an artifact instead of answering inline?
flashcards.back: When the content is substantial and self-contained (usually more than about 15 lines) and likely to be edited, reused, or shared.

flashcards.front: When should you ask for structured data (table, CSV, JSON) output?
flashcards.back: When the output feeds a spreadsheet or system, or items must be compared field by field. Name the fields, set a 'not stated' value, and spot-check rows.

flashcards.front: After Claude adapts a draft for a new audience, what must you check?
flashcards.back: That facts, figures, hedges, caveats, and commitments are unchanged. Simplifying often turns estimates into promises.

flashcards.front: How should you choose between several Claude drafts?
flashcards.back: Score them against criteria set in advance (accuracy to source, key messages, audience fit, risk), then verify the chosen one. Not by length or confidence.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: the three parts of Description?
flashcards.back: Product (what you want: output, format, audience, style), Process (how to approach it), and Performance (how Claude should behave during the collaboration).

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: the three parts of Discernment?
flashcards.back: Product discernment (output quality), Process discernment (soundness of the reasoning), and Performance discernment (whether the communication style works for you).

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: the three parts of Diligence?
flashcards.back: Creation (which AI you use and how), Transparency (being honest about AI's role with those who need to know), and Deployment (verifying and vouching for outputs you share).

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: the three interaction modes?
flashcards.back: Automation (AI executes a defined task), Augmentation (human and AI think together iteratively), and Agency (human configures AI to work independently).

flashcards.front: AI Fluency definition of bias in AI output?
flashcards.back: Systematic patterns that unfairly favour or disadvantage certain groups or perspectives, often reflecting patterns in training data.

flashcards.front: Is the 4D framework an official CCAO-F objective?
flashcards.back: No. It's a teaching lens from Anthropic's AI Fluency course. The exam objectives test the same skills (evaluation, verification, accountability) without naming it.

flashcards.front: Opus vs. Sonnet vs. Haiku in one line each.
flashcards.back: Opus: most capable, for complex work. Sonnet: balanced speed and intelligence. Haiku: fastest and lowest-cost, for simple or high-volume tasks such as classification and extraction.

flashcards.front: Rule of thumb for model choice?
flashcards.back: Use the smallest model that reliably meets your quality bar. Move up a tier when quality matters more than speed or limits.

flashcards.front: When do you use web search?
flashcards.back: For current information, recent events, and anything after the model's training cutoff, and when you want cited sources.

flashcards.front: Web search vs. Research?
flashcards.back: Web search: quick factual lookups (one or two searches) with citations. Research: a deeper multi-step investigation across many sources (and connected tools) that produces a longer cited report. Slower, paid plans, and uses limits faster.

flashcards.front: What is extended thinking (or higher effort) for?
flashcards.back: Giving Claude more reasoning room on complex analysis, planning, logic, or math that doesn't need recent web information. Unnecessary for simple tasks, where it only adds time and usage.

flashcards.front: What are artifacts?
flashcards.back: Substantial standalone outputs beside the chat (documents, code, diagrams, interactive apps) that you can iterate on and, depending on settings, share.

flashcards.front: What is Claude Code?
flashcards.back: Anthropic's agentic coding tool that reads codebases, edits files, and runs commands for software tasks. A developer surface: Associates recognise the need and escalate rather than configure it.

flashcards.front: Individual vs. organizational plans?
flashcards.back: Free, Pro, Max, and Ultra are individual plans. Team and Enterprise add central admin, SSO, governance controls, and commercial data terms. Verify current plans.

flashcards.front: What does Claude in Chrome do (conceptually)?
flashcards.back: It's a browser extension (paid plans) that lets Claude read web pages and take actions in the browser. Prompt injection from pages is the biggest risk, so use trusted sites and keep sensitive accounts separate.

flashcards.front: Best surface for drafting campaign copy?
flashcards.back: The Claude app (web or desktop), ideally inside a Project with brand guidelines. Not Claude Code.

flashcards.front: When does code execution and file creation help?
flashcards.back: For accurate data analysis on uploaded files and for creating files such as spreadsheets, documents, and slides. The setting is now labelled "Create and edit files".

flashcards.front: Web search vs. extended thinking: which needs the internet?
flashcards.back: Web search, for current facts. Extended thinking is for complex reasoning that doesn't require recent information from the web.

flashcards.front: What does the effort setting control in the Claude apps?
flashcards.back: How much work Claude puts into a response, from Low (routine) to Max (deepest analysis). Higher effort uses more tokens and more of your usage limit.

flashcards.front: A model always thinks and has no thinking toggle. How do you get a faster, lighter answer?
flashcards.back: Lower the effort level, or switch to a lighter model for the task.

flashcards.front: What is Claude Tag?
flashcards.back: The Slack integration: @Claude in a channel and results post in the thread. Team and Enterprise plans only. Team work in shared channels is Claude Tag; personal work on your own files is Cowork (now part of the unified Claude app) or Claude Code.

flashcards.front: Two cautions for Claude for Excel?
flashcards.back: Use it only with trusted spreadsheets (prompt-injection risk), and don't use it for final client deliverables or audit-critical calculations without human review and verification.

flashcards.front: A stakeholder wants Claude embedded in the company's customer portal. What's the Associate's move?
flashcards.back: Recognise it as API or developer work and escalate it to developers or architects. Associates don't build against the API.

flashcards.front: Restart, summarize, or persist: when do you start a new chat?
flashcards.back: When the topic changes, or a long thread has drifted, picked up wrong assumptions, or become slow and unfocused.

flashcards.front: How do you carry work from a long chat into a fresh one?
flashcards.back: Ask Claude for a concise summary of decisions, open questions, and key facts, check it, then paste it into the new chat.

flashcards.front: Where should context you reuse across many chats live?
flashcards.back: Stable reference material and instructions in a Project; personal preferences and ongoing context in memory.

flashcards.front: Context window vs. usage limit?
flashcards.back: Context window: how much one conversation can hold. Usage limit: how much you can use Claude over a period, shared across surfaces.

flashcards.front: What does a Project contain?
flashcards.back: A set of chats plus shared project knowledge (documents) and project instructions (custom instructions) that apply to every chat in it.

flashcards.front: What does sharing a Project with your team do?
flashcards.back: It standardizes a workflow: teammates use the same knowledge and instructions. Available on Team and Enterprise plans, with "Can view" or "Can edit" access.

flashcards.front: Five things to map when designing a Claude workflow?
flashcards.back: Inputs, Claude's steps, human checkpoints, outputs and destinations, and failure or uncertainty handling.

flashcards.front: What are connectors?
flashcards.back: Integrations that give Claude live, permissioned access to external apps and data (Drive, email, calendar, CRM, etc.). Built on MCP.

flashcards.front: What is MCP?
flashcards.back: The Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources.

flashcards.front: Whose permissions does Claude use through a connector?
flashcards.back: Yours. It can access what your account can access in that system.

flashcards.front: Least privilege for connectors means…
flashcards.back: Enabling only the connectors (and scopes) a specific task needs.

flashcards.front: Where should humans stay in a Claude workflow?
flashcards.back: On judgment, approval, accountability, and irreversible or external actions.

flashcards.front: Why not upload daily manual CRM exports if a connector exists?
flashcards.back: Exports go stale, multiply copies of sensitive data, and sit outside the source system's access controls. An approved connector gives live access within your existing permissions.

flashcards.front: Safe rollout of an AI-drafted customer reply workflow?
flashcards.back: Start with human review of every draft, measure quality, and reduce oversight only where it's proven safe and policy allows.

flashcards.front: When should you use Research rather than web search?
flashcards.back: For broad, multi-source investigation that produces a longer report with citations. Use web search for simple, factual lookups. Research is paid-plan only and uses more of your limit.

flashcards.front: What can the Gmail connector do, and what is the default safeguard?
flashcards.back: Search, read, draft, send, reply and forward. By default Claude asks for your approval before each action.

flashcards.front: What does the Google Drive connector read?
flashcards.back: Docs, Sheets, Slides and PDFs you have access to. It extracts text, so content only in images or charts may be missed.

flashcards.front: Three things to tell stakeholders about a Claude workflow?
flashcards.back: The value (ideally measured in a pilot), the limitations (hallucination, bias, knowledge cutoff), and the controls (human review, data access, escalation).

flashcards.front: Augment vs. redesign a process: which first?
flashcards.back: Usually augment: add Claude to steps of the existing process. Redesign the process around Claude once quality and fit are proven.

flashcards.front: Do scheduled tasks remove the need for a human checkpoint?
flashcards.back: No. They automate when the work runs. A person still reviews outputs before they are sent or acted on.

flashcards.front: How can Claude-made Docs and Slides fit existing team tools?
flashcards.back: Docs export to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs. Slides export to PowerPoint or PDF, or can be sent to Google Slides.

flashcards.front: How should you treat Claude's process-optimisation suggestions?
flashcards.back: As hypotheses: validate bottlenecks and automation ideas with the people who do the work, and pilot before rolling out.

flashcards.front: Account-wide instructions vs. project instructions?
flashcards.back: Account-wide "Instructions for Claude" (Settings > Your Claude) apply to all your chats. Project instructions apply only within that Project.

flashcards.front: The "Use style" menu is deprecated in Claude chat. How do you control tone and format now?
flashcards.back: Describe tone and format in account-wide or project instructions (a short sample helps), or package a repeatable format in a Skill.

flashcards.front: How do you get Claude to write in your own voice across all chats?
flashcards.back: Add a description of your voice, with a short writing sample, to your account-wide instructions. Use project instructions if it only applies to one workflow.

flashcards.front: What is memory in Claude?
flashcards.back: Claude's ability to remember relevant context from past chats, stored as topics you can view and edit. You can pause or reset it, and incognito chats aren't saved to memory.

flashcards.front: What are Skills?
flashcards.back: Folders of instructions (plus optional scripts and resources) that Claude loads only when relevant, for repeatable procedures like company document formats. They require code execution.

flashcards.front: Skill vs. Project instructions?
flashcards.back: Project instructions apply to one Project's chats. A Skill is a reusable procedure Claude pulls in on demand, wherever it's relevant.

flashcards.front: Top knowledge-hygiene practice?
flashcards.back: Remove or clearly mark outdated and conflicting documents, version file names, and assign an owner who reviews them on a schedule.

flashcards.front: Risk of sensitive docs in a shared Project?
flashcards.back: Every member of the Project can effectively access that content through Claude. Only include what all members may see.

flashcards.front: Where should team-critical business rules live?
flashcards.back: In explicit, reviewable shared project instructions or a Skill, not in individual memory.

flashcards.front: What does a connector (e.g., Google Drive or Gmail) let Claude access?
flashcards.back: Live content in that tool, limited to what the signed-in user can already access. Access mirrors the user's existing permissions.

flashcards.front: Upload to project knowledge or use a connector?
flashcards.back: Upload a stable, approved reference version. Connect a source when Claude needs its current state because it changes often.

flashcards.front: What happens when project knowledge nears the context limit on a paid plan?
flashcards.back: Claude switches to retrieval (RAG), pulling in the most relevant passages so the Project can hold much more material.

flashcards.front: Shared Project access levels (Team/Enterprise)?
flashcards.back: "Can view" or "Can edit". Editors can change instructions and knowledge and manage members.

flashcards.front: How do you fully isolate a Project's memory from your other work?
flashcards.back: Each Project has its own memory but also uses account memory. Turn off "Use account memory" for that Project.

flashcards.front: Pausing memory vs. resetting memory?
flashcards.back: Pausing stops new memories but keeps existing ones. Resetting deletes all memories.

flashcards.front: Where are incognito chats available, and what do they skip?
flashcards.back: Only outside Projects. They aren't saved to history or memory and are excluded from chat search, but still follow Team/Enterprise retention settings.

flashcards.front: Can Team/Enterprise Owners read members' memories?
flashcards.back: No. Owners control memory org-wide (and turning it off deletes entries), but they cannot view members' memories.

flashcards.front: What should trigger a review of a Project's instructions and knowledge?
flashcards.back: Changes to the underlying facts (new policy, pricing, process) as well as a regular schedule, followed by re-testing with known prompts.

flashcards.front: Safety rule for custom Skills and custom connectors?
flashcards.back: Only use ones from trusted sources. Custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic.

flashcards.front: AI Fluency: Diligence means…
flashcards.back: Taking responsibility for AI-assisted work: thoughtful tool choice, transparency about AI use, and verifying before deploying.

flashcards.front: First question before pasting data into Claude?
flashcards.back: What classification is this data, and is this tool or workspace approved for it under company policy?

flashcards.front: What is data minimization?
flashcards.back: Sharing only what the task needs, and removing or pseudonymizing identifiers such as names, emails, and account numbers.

flashcards.front: Why use the company workspace instead of a personal account?
flashcards.back: Organizational plans have admin controls, SSO, commercial data terms, and governance. Personal accounts bypass them.

flashcards.front: What is Anthropic's Usage Policy?
flashcards.back: Anthropic's rules for using its products: universal prohibitions (e.g., malware, fraud, privacy violations, deceptive campaigns), extra requirements for high-risk uses that affect people (e.g., legal, medical, finance, employment, credit, housing), and further use-case guidelines.

flashcards.front: What is prompt injection?
flashcards.back: Malicious or misleading instructions hidden in content Claude reads (web pages, emails, documents) that try to hijack its behavior.

flashcards.front: Who is accountable for AI-assisted work?
flashcards.back: The human or organization that uses, sends, or decides based on it. Accountability doesn't transfer to the AI.

flashcards.front: When should meaningful human review be required?
flashcards.back: For external or customer-facing, regulated (legal, financial, medical), people-affecting, or irreversible outputs and actions.

flashcards.front: What makes human review 'meaningful'?
flashcards.back: The reviewer has the expertise, time, and authority to change or reject the output. A rubber stamp doesn't count.

flashcards.front: When should you disclose AI involvement?
flashcards.back: Per policy and regulation, and whenever the audience would reasonably expect to know (published content, customer-facing AI, professional work norms).

flashcards.front: IT approval for a connector is slow. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Follow the approval process. Never install unapproved integrations (shadow AI).

flashcards.front: Usage Policy: what two requirements apply to high-risk uses that affect people?
flashcards.back: Human-in-the-loop (a qualified person meaningfully reviews the AI recommendation with authority to change it) and disclosure (the affected person is told AI was used).

flashcards.front: What must a consumer-facing chatbot built on Claude tell its users?
flashcards.back: That they're interacting with AI rather than a human.

flashcards.front: Name three kinds of use the Usage Policy prohibits for everyone.
flashcards.back: Examples: creating malware or gaining unauthorized access, fraud and deceptive campaigns, privacy or identity violations, surveillance, disinformation, and jailbreaking or other platform abuse.

flashcards.front: Is customer content on Team, Enterprise, or the API used to train Anthropic's models by default?
flashcards.back: No. Commercial terms say customer content isn't used for training by default. Company data policy still applies.

flashcards.front: On consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max, Ultra), who decides whether chats can be used for model training?
flashcards.back: The user, through a privacy setting. Retention length depends on that choice.

flashcards.front: What can Team and Enterprise admins set for each connector or tool?
flashcards.back: Always allow, Needs approval, or Blocked.

flashcards.front: Which admin controls are Enterprise-only (vs. Team)?
flashcards.back: SCIM provisioning, audit logs, the Compliance API, custom data retention, and custom roles. SSO is on both Team and Enterprise.

flashcards.front: Does telling Claude "don't retain this data" satisfy a data policy?
flashcards.back: No. An instruction in the chat isn't a data control. Remove or anonymize restricted identifiers before uploading.

flashcards.front: You accidentally pasted an API key into a chat. What now?
flashcards.back: Treat it as exposed: report per policy and rotate or revoke the key. In future, replace secrets with placeholders.

flashcards.front: Can a Team or Enterprise Owner read a member's individual memories?
flashcards.back: No. Owners can turn memory on or off org-wide, but they can't view members' memories.

flashcards.front: Output is generic. Most likely cause?
flashcards.back: Missing context, audience, or success criteria. Add them, plus an example.

flashcards.front: Claude ignores one instruction. First diagnosis?
flashcards.back: Check whether it's buried, conflicting with another instruction, or unexplained. Fix placement and conflicts, and give the reason.

flashcards.front: A long chat starts forgetting earlier details. Fix?
flashcards.back: Ask for a summary of decisions and open items, start a new chat with it, and move stable reference material into a Project.

flashcards.front: Three ways to stretch usage limits?
flashcards.back: Use a lighter model for simple tasks, avoid re-sending large files and long threads, and batch related questions into one well-structured message.

flashcards.front: Will a bigger model fix missing company context?
flashcards.back: No. A model can't know facts you didn't provide. Add the context first.

flashcards.front: Best practice when refining a prompt?
flashcards.back: Change one variable at a time and test on the same representative examples.

flashcards.front: Output is consistently too long. Fixes?
flashcards.back: Specify the length and format explicitly (e.g., 'under 120 words, 3 bullets'). For a lasting preference, add it to account or project instructions.

flashcards.front: Usage limit vs. length limit?
flashcards.back: Usage limits cap consumption over time (a session window plus weekly limits, shared across Claude apps). The length limit is the context window of one conversation.

flashcards.front: Name four things that use more of your usage limit.
flashcards.back: Any four of: long messages, large attachments, long conversations, Research and web search, higher effort or thinking, artifacts, multi-step tasks.

flashcards.front: Why keep repeated reference files in Project knowledge instead of re-uploading them?
flashcards.back: Project content is cached, so reusing it counts less against your limit. Re-uploading into new chats costs the full amount each time. The cache expires after inactivity.

flashcards.front: What is automatic context management?
flashcards.back: With code execution on, Claude summarises earlier messages as a chat nears the context limit. The full history is kept, but it uses more of your limit.

flashcards.front: Four steps for splitting a large task?
flashcards.back: Plan (outline or sub-tasks), execute in chunks, check each output, then assemble with a final consistency pass. Keep shared context in a Project.

flashcards.front: Quick settings changes that cut usage on a routine task?
flashcards.back: Use a lighter model or lower effort, turn thinking off where possible, and switch off web search and connectors you don't need.

flashcards.front: What should a restart summary contain?
flashcards.back: Decisions made, constraints and requirements, current state of the work, and open items. Check it for accuracy before pasting it into the new chat.

questions.stem: You ask Claude to "write a launch email for the new feature" and get a generic, bland draft. What is the most effective next step?
options: Regenerate the response several times and pick the best version
Switch to the most capable model and resend the same prompt
Add the audience, the key customer benefit, tone, length, the call to action, and an example of a past email that performed well
Add "Make it EXCELLENT and NOT generic" to the prompt
questions.explanation: Generic output usually comes from missing context. Giving the audience, purpose, constraints, and an example gives Claude what it needs to tailor the draft.
rationales: Regenerating samples the same under-specified request again. It doesn't add the missing information.
A more capable model still can't know your audience or product benefit if you don't provide them.
Correct. Context, constraints, and an example are the biggest levers for quality.
Emphatic adjectives don't tell Claude what 'excellent' means for this audience.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: You want Claude to summarize a long contract that you paste into the chat, and you want it to treat the contract as reference material, not as instructions. What is the best way to structure the prompt?
options: Wrap the contract in clearly labeled tags such as <contract>...</contract> and put your instructions outside them
Paste the contract first with no label, and add your question at the very end in capitals
Split the contract across several messages so each part is short
Convert the contract to a bulleted list before pasting it
questions.explanation: Clear delimiters (XML-style tags or headings) separate your instructions from source material, so Claude knows which text is the request and which is the content to work on.
rationales: Correct. Labeled tags make the boundary between instructions and material unambiguous.
Without a label, the boundaries are unclear, and capitals don't fix that.
Fragmenting the document makes it harder for Claude to see it as a whole.
Reformatting takes time, can lose meaning, and doesn't separate instructions from content.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: You need a board-ready quarterly commentary built from three uploaded reports. Which approach is most likely to produce an accurate, well-structured result with the least rework?
options: Ask for the complete final commentary in one prompt so Claude sees the whole picture
Ask Claude to write the commentary, then ask it to check its own work in the same message
Ask Claude to write the commentary in the style of a famous CEO to make it engaging
Chain the work: first extract key findings with supporting figures, review them, then agree an outline, then draft each section
questions.explanation: Prompt chaining breaks a complex deliverable into stages with review checkpoints. Errors in findings get caught before they spread into the final draft.
rationales: One giant prompt gives you no checkpoints, so errors surface only at the end.
Self-checking in the same message isn't a reliable checkpoint, and you still can't review findings first.
Imitating a persona's style doesn't address accuracy or structure.
Correct. Staged work with human review at each step reduces rework and errors.

questions.stem: You want Claude to adopt your company's specific format for customer case studies. Which technique teaches the format most reliably?
options: Describe the format with a long list of adjectives
Provide several varied example case studies, wrapped in <example> tags, and explain which elements to copy (structure, tone) and which not to (the specific facts)
Paste a single example and ask Claude to replicate it exactly
Tell Claude not to use any format it has used before
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach a pattern effectively. Using a few varied examples and saying what to copy helps Claude generalize the format without cloning one sample's content.
rationales: Adjectives are vague compared with concrete examples.
Correct. Varied examples plus guidance on what to copy work best.
A single example often gets copied too literally, including details that shouldn't carry over.
A negative instruction gives no target format.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: HR policy assistant in a Project
questions.stem: You're drafting an employee FAQ for a new hybrid-work policy and aren't sure what information Claude needs. What is the most efficient way to start?
options: Ask Claude to write the FAQ immediately and fix it later
Spend an hour writing a perfect prompt before involving Claude
Share the policy and ask Claude to first ask you up to five clarifying questions about audience, scope, and edge cases before drafting
Ask Claude to find a hybrid-work FAQ from another company and copy it
questions.explanation: Inviting clarifying questions quickly surfaces missing context (audience, regions, exceptions) and makes the first draft far more useful.
rationales: Drafting without the key context usually leads to many rounds of rework.
Over-engineering the prompt upfront is slow. Claude can help identify what matters.
Correct. Clarifying questions surface missing assumptions efficiently.
Copying another company's FAQ doesn't reflect your policy, and may raise copyright and accuracy issues.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A report summary will be read aloud by a text-to-speech system. Which instruction is most likely to produce suitable output?
options: Don't use bullets, tables, or symbols.
Format the summary as you normally would.
NEVER EVER use formatting.
Write in short, flowing spoken-style paragraphs without symbols or lists, because this will be read aloud by a text-to-speech system.
questions.explanation: Positive instructions plus a reason work best. Knowing the output will be read aloud lets Claude handle cases the rule didn't spell out, such as abbreviations and numbers.
rationales: It says what to avoid but not what to do, and gives no reason.
Normal formatting likely includes lists and symbols that read badly aloud.
Shouting doesn't add clarity or the reason for the rule.
Correct. It's a positive instruction with the reason behind it.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Using the AI Fluency framework, which activity is the best example of DELEGATION?
options: Checking Claude's draft against the source policy for accuracy
Writing a detailed prompt describing the desired tone and format
Disclosing to readers that a report was prepared with AI assistance
Deciding that Claude will draft the first version of the training guide while you decide which policy positions to take
questions.explanation: Delegation is deciding whether, what, and how much of the work to hand to AI, while keeping the judgment-heavy parts with the human.
rationales: That is Discernment: evaluating output.
That is Description: communicating what you want.
That is part of Diligence: transparency and responsibility.
Correct. Dividing work between human and AI is Delegation.

sources.title: AI Fluency — Anthropic

questions.stem: After six rounds of revisions, a chat about a pricing proposal has drifted: it's built on a discount assumption you later rejected, and Claude keeps reintroducing it. What should you do? (Select two.)
options: Keep correcting the assumption in each new message
Ask Claude for a concise summary of the decisions you actually agreed on, excluding the rejected discount assumption
Switch to a lighter model to reduce confusion
Start a new chat with a consolidated prompt that includes the corrected assumptions and the agreed decisions
questions.explanation: When a thread is polluted by a rejected assumption, summarize the valid decisions and start fresh with a clean, consolidated prompt. That removes the rejected context Claude keeps picking up.
rationales: The rejected assumption stays in the thread's context, so it keeps resurfacing.
Correct. A clean summary captures what's still valid.
Model size isn't the cause. The polluted context is.
Correct. A fresh chat with corrected context stops the old assumption from influencing output.

sources.title: Usage and length limits — Claude Help

questions.stem: You need Claude to recommend which of three CRM rollout plans to pursue. Which prompt addition most improves the quality of its recommendation?
options: Ask Claude to compare each plan against cost, risk, adoption effort, and time-to-value before giving a recommendation with its reasoning
Ask Claude to answer in one word so it's decisive
Ask Claude to pick the plan most companies choose
Ask Claude to recommend whichever plan is listed first
questions.explanation: Asking Claude to reason through explicit criteria before concluding produces a more thoughtful, inspectable recommendation.
rationales: Correct. Explicit criteria and visible reasoning improve quality and let you check the logic.
A one-word answer hides the reasoning and invites shallow judgment.
Popularity isn't a decision criterion for your context, and Claude may not know it reliably.
That's arbitrary and ignores the analysis entirely.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Which elements belong in a well-specified prompt for a customer-facing apology email about a service outage? (Select three.)
options: The audience and desired tone (e.g., affected enterprise customers; accountable, non-defensive)
A request that Claude invent a plausible root cause if none is known yet
What happened and what is being done to fix it, using confirmed facts you provide
An instruction to promise a full refund to make customers happy
Constraints such as length, and commitments the company has approved (and must not exceed)
questions.explanation: Good prompts supply verified facts, the audience and tone, and constraints, including which commitments are approved. Inventing causes or unapproved promises creates legal and trust risk.
rationales: Correct. Audience and tone shape an apology's effectiveness.
Inventing a root cause is fabrication and can mislead customers.
Correct. Confirmed facts ground the email.
Unapproved commitments create financial and legal exposure.
Correct. Limits and approved commitments prevent overpromising.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: You upload an 80-page vendor contract and want to know the termination notice period and any penalties. Which prompt setup is most likely to give an accurate answer you can quickly verify?
options: Put your question first, then paste the contract text below it
Attach the contract, then at the end ask Claude to first quote the clauses on termination and penalties, and answer using only those quotes
Paste your own one-page summary of the contract to save Claude reading time
Ask Claude what notice periods are typical for vendor contracts
questions.explanation: For long documents, placing the material first and the question last, and asking for relevant quotes before the answer, anchors Claude to the actual text. The quotes also let you check the answer against the contract quickly.
rationales: Question-first ordering tends to work worse on long inputs, and nothing anchors the answer to specific clauses.
Correct. Document first, question last, and quote-first grounding produce a checkable answer.
Your summary may omit the exact clause wording that matters, and the answer can't be traced to the contract.
Typical terms say nothing about what this specific contract says.

questions.stem: You need product names for a new feature. Your first prompt, "Give me the best name," returns one safe, forgettable option. What is the best way to restructure the work?
options: Ask for 30 varied names across different styles without judging them, then in a second step score the shortlist against criteria such as memorability, fit with the brand, and clarity
Regenerate the same prompt until a name you like appears
Ask Claude to answer only with the single most creative name possible
Ask Claude to use the names competitors chose as a template
questions.explanation: Brainstorming works best as a two-step chain: generate many varied options first, then narrow with explicit criteria. Asking for one 'best' answer collapses both steps and invites a safe, generic result.
rationales: Correct. Volume and variety first, then filtering against stated criteria.
Regenerating samples the same under-specified request and gives no criteria to judge by.
One answer, with 'creative' undefined, repeats the same problem.
Copying competitors' naming patterns works against differentiation and adds no criteria.

questions.scenario: HR policy assistant in a Project
questions.stem: You are building a recurring prompt that turns raw interview notes into a hiring-panel summary. Which additions most improve consistency and quality? (Select two.)
options: Explicit success criteria, such as: each competency rated with one quoted piece of evidence, under 250 words, no comments about personal characteristics
Three to five varied example summaries, wrapped in <example> tags, with a note to copy the structure but not the content
The instruction "Be thorough and professional" in capital letters
A request that Claude infer each candidate's age and family situation to give fuller context
questions.explanation: Explicit success criteria define what a good summary looks like, and several varied examples teach the format reliably. Emphasis without specifics adds nothing, and inferring personal characteristics is inappropriate in hiring and creates fairness and legal risk.
rationales: Correct. Clear criteria make output consistent and checkable.
Correct. Varied examples teach the structure without cloning one sample's content.
Capitals and vague adjectives don't say what 'thorough' means here.
Inferring protected or personal characteristics is inappropriate for hiring decisions and introduces bias.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: You ask Claude to critique a project plan, and the feedback is polite and shallow. Which single change is most likely to produce sharper, more useful critique?
options: Switch to a different chat and paste the same request
Ask Claude to be nicer so it feels comfortable criticizing
Ask for a longer response
Give Claude a role and a lens, such as "You are an experienced delivery lead reviewing this plan for schedule and dependency risks. List the three biggest risks and why."
questions.explanation: A role statement focuses Claude's behavior and tone, and naming the lens and output format tells it what kind of critique you want. Even one sentence of role can noticeably change the result.
rationales: The same request in a new chat lacks the same missing direction.
Tone encouragement doesn't define what to look for.
Length doesn't create depth. It often adds padding.
Correct. A role plus a specific lens and output shape gives a focused critique.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs
